THE SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION

Oral History
Interview with Jimmy Crawford by Stanley Crouch
Cassettes 1-2

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
AREA CODE 202 347-5395

PMcC
P R O C E E D I N G S
MR. CROUCH: Interview with Mr. Jimmy Crawford, February 12th, 1978, at his home, 3240 Maryland Avenue in the West Bronx.
Right.
Okay. Now, Mr. Crawford, since this interview is supposed to deal with your life and career as a musician, I think we should start --
At the beginning.
Yeah, right.
(Laughter)
Well, I don't -- is it necessary to call your name?
Do what you want to do.

Well, Stanley, I started out in Memphis, Tennessee, in high school under Jimmy Lansford's band, and I'm going back around about '28 and '29 now, and so we formed a little amateur high school orchestra, and so -- well, I just knew I was going (Inaudible), my mother, dad died when I was six, five or six. I was raised by my grandparents, who could neither read nor write. And she was the greatest midwife in the city of Memphis. She assisted in delivering more babies than any doctor in Memphis, white or colored, and also I mean Black or white babies. She didn't just deliver Blacks only or Negroes, I prefer to say, or colored.

Now, this woman was an amazing lady, without any formal education whatsoever, because she couldn't write, read nor write. My grandfather was the same a saint. They were the only parents I had besides an aunt, who's dead now, who lived across the street, and one of my grandfather's (inaudible).

Now, I started out, as I forestated, with an orchestra leader (inaudible). He was an athletic instructor there, Jimmy Lunsford. He finished Fisk University, and then he came to New York. Pardon me. He took up postgraduate work at Columbia University, and also he tried to join Fletcher Henderson's band, but he didn't make it.

So he came back to Memphis. Now, he finished Fisk University, which was in Nashville, but he came back to Memphis to accept a job there as athletic instructor. The man was a natural athlete, a good musician, and above all he was one of the greatest gentlemen that I ever met in my life. I loved the man. He's dead now, of course, and we started out from scratch.

And all of a sudden -- we used to go to Lakeside, Ohio. That's right off Lake Erie, right on Lake Erie -- for about three or four summer seasons, and finally round about 1929, Stanley, we decided to go North, you know, go further north. So we went to Cleveland, Ohio. We had a job there to go on, Willie's Lakeshore Garden. That was the most popular place in Cleveland.

But when we got to Cleveland, they had -- there was a musician's strike and a waiter's strike on just simultaneously, at the same time, and I'm telling you, we laid around Cleveland, starving, nothing, because when you go to bed with nothing and hungry, you're bound to wake up with nothing and hungry.

So I -- or we rather -- we took it upon ourselves to go around trying to look on the streets and find a penny so we could buy a penny's worth of peanuts and drink some water behind it and then you're full. Well, that's what I did, tried to find me some pennies, insert in those salted peanut machines they had in those days, drink some water behind it. Nobody gave me nothing.

I know they didn't give me anything. Lunsford starved, himself. And my wife was working with a fellow by the name of Ralph Cooper, who used to take shows on the road, playing the colored theaters and whatnot and clubs, and, well, Ralph had a little bit more incentive about him at that time. He would go in a town, and he would go and make arrangements with the owner of some restaurant where his employees or his dancing chorus line and fellows and acts and et cetera, they would go in and eat and then sign their name. Lunsford didn't do that for us.
Well, he -- we all were inexperienced, and I remember -- and so we finally left Cleveland and went over to
Buffalo, still starving and --
How did you get from Cleveland to Buffalo?

Automobile, a Ford, little Ford, 1920 -- oh, this was 1933 then, because I stayed in Cleveland and Cincinnati starving, man. I'm telling you. I was too proud to ask. I always had a little -- held my head up high. I was just a proud man.
So this was from 19 -- so you were in Cleveland from 1929 to 1933?

I was in Lakeside, Ohio. That was the last year we were in Lakeside, Ohio, playing at this summer resort. So we decided to migrate north. So we went to Cleveland, right around Lake Erie, and then we got to Cleveland, and I just told you what happened.
Now, what year -- you got to Cleveland in 1929?

Well, yeah, around 1929. I stayed there between Cleveland, Cincinnati and the territories around in there, and I -- we stayed around in that vicinity and finally wound up in Buffalo, New York. I stayed in Buffalo from 1933 --'32 or '33, and then we finally came to New York. Then our first big break was the Cotton Club on Lenox Avenue, which was owned by (inaudible) Mike [Bass], Herman Steeks. I'm going into detail. Now, they can erase it if they wish.
the old Cotton Club
Cuney Madden,
Starks
But they -- that was the most popular club in New York.
Okay, now let's -- before we get into the Cotton Club -- now, all of you -- all of you left together when you came to Buffalo?
Oh, yes, we were one solid unit.
So you were there about three -- in the territories between Cleveland and Cincinnati and around there -- you all were there about three years.
Just about, because we got into -- into New York on about 1933, and they put us in the Cotton Club.
Right, now -- so now, the three years that you were in Cleveland and Cincinnati --
The territory.
-- the territory -- did you all work much?

Whenever we could get a job, and then when we got a job, Stanley, the booker would run off with the money. I remember one real rainy night in Cleveland the booker ran away with the money we were getting the money from a private gig that Jimmie Lunsford played in the band. He tore out in his car, raining like mad. And so Lunsford, myself and a fellow, pianist, piano player by the name of Eddie Wilcox, we were in Lunsford's Ford.

And we stayed right on his tail. And so we finally caught him, and so he said, well, here, man. Here's your money. Naturally, we wanted to jump on the guy, but we was too well bred for that, because he didn't know who you -- you know, what you were running into when you jumped down a man and jump on his back and try to do him in.

Well, we got paid. In the meantime, while in Cleveland still a-starving -- this was in, 'round about 1931 or '32 -- Colored, nice looking woman by the name of Brown, Bobbie Brown, pianist, oh, you know, well, she needed a drummer one night. It was just the two of us, Bobbie Brown and Jimmy Crawford.

So I accepted the gig, naturally. I was hungry. And so she gave me $19.00 for the gig. That was more money than I ever had in my life. Me in turn took that -- took part of it or most of it and bought up a whole bag of hot dogs and threw some peanuts in there also, can't get away from those peanuts, and went back to the Majestic Hotel, woke everybody up in the band and said, hey, fellows, let's eat. Whole bag, a bag two feet tall or something like that.
And we sat and ate the hot dogs, baby, and that was my -- oh, that was like a (inaudible) featured meal. And we ate it. Then eventually we tripped on over to Buffalo, New York --
Now, I wanted to -- before we go to
New York, I wanted to go back some and deal with your earlier life as a drummer.
Oh, I'd like to tell you something.
Okay.

Stanley, my inspiration to become a drummer was a fellow who inspired me to no end, the utmost in sensational drumming, was a drummer by the name of Booker Washington at the Palace Theater. He was in the pit, only had about seven, eight pieces, but my aunt used to take me to the Palace Theater once a week so I could see this drummer. Boy, that man, wow, who played the Palace Theater -- Butterbeans and Susie, (inaudible) Ma Rainey, Bessie Smith, all those type of people.
Well, how was the theater built? What did it look like?
Oh, the Palace Theater on Beale Street? It was just a Negro theater, you know, and just -- four walls and a roof over it.
Did it have a balcony?
I can't remember, can't recall right now, but apparently it was for cheap prices for admittance.
You remember how much it cost to get in?
Oh, about 35 or something like that, and I think that may have been tops. But this drummer had sticks on -- rolling around in his fingers like wheels,

throwing them in the air, and I always said in the present day that no drummer can play drums with the sticks in the air, but it happened then with this fellow in Memphis. Booker Washington, later on he died. He went to New Orleans, then came back to Memphis, and then he went to Chicago, and he passed there from pneumonia or tuberculosis.

Well, me, that man inspired me so much that I didn't want to be nothing but a drummer. I've got some more to tell you later years (inaudible). Why, Lunceford and I had a big argument. We were in some theater playing with Bill Robinson Enwright. This was after we had got to New York and were in the Cotton Club. And we got in a heck of an argument, heated argument. Of course, Lunceford was such a gentleman, he wouldn't dare fight or nothing like that, no -- I was quarterback on his football team and half -- halfback in Memphis at Manassas High School where he was a physical ed. man. He was a great athlete and a great gentleman. I don't know why I got so angry with Lunceford. On second thought I do know why, because Lunceford didn't ever buy his band's uniforms.
(Laughter)

Cab Calloway, Duke Ellington and the big bands like that -- well, Cab Calloway and Duke Ellington I knew. On top of that, Stanley, I went in behind Cab Calloway, Lunceford's band did, while Sammy Greer -- you know him -- he was playing drums for Duke Ellington, and all the drummers that appeared

in the Cotton Club with those bands had fabulous drum outfits, gongs, chimes, vibraphones, timpanies, all kind of drums hanging around. It was a beautiful setting for those bands. Well, Stocks told Harold Oxley and Jimmie Lunsford, now, your drummer got to have some drums up there. I was sitting up there with a bass drum and one cymbal. He said, no, we used to seeing drums in here, make a beautiful setting for the band.

So went to work and I, you know, I took it upon myself to go and buy a whole complete set of Leedy drums like Sonny Greer and Manzie and Cab, like what they had, and they did set the band off. It looked beautiful, took me a day to set them up.

And so I had to pay for them. I think it was around about 1,600.00. Now, I'm making about $60.00 a week, and I got pretty burned up about that, plus Lunsford never bought any uniforms or paid for the uniforms that we wore in his band to make his band impressive.

So I just got filled up, and Bill Robinson in some theater, now -- I can't recall what theater we were in -- this man, after he heard me out there telling Lunsford off -- and I'm telling the God's truth -- he gave his -- told his valet, name was Billy, give me some money, give me some money. So he came out and told Lunsford, here -- wonder can I use this word I'm going to use.
Oh, you can use any word you want to. I hope they erase it

All right (inaudible), which I don't like that word myself, and I don't like the word hate, I say I dislike. So he says, here, here, Jimmie. Pay that nigger off over there and let him go; turn him loose. Who needs him?

Now, this man had no business saying that. He wasn't any part of Lunsford's band. He was just a featured actor, buck dancer, I called him. He's dead now. Soon as I get a chance, I'm going to throw another shovel of dirt in his face, on his grave.
(Laughter)
And I mean it.

I disliked that man so much, until I'm going to use the word hate. He didn't have any business butting in Lunsford's business. Lunsford politely told him, said, now, let him alone, let him alone. I'll take care of that. Say, we're together; we started out together. We're going to stay together as long as he want to stay here.

Now, I drummed with Lunsford's band for 14 years, and the reason I got out of the band, Uncle Sam called me. So I was behind my drum right over there at Camp Kilmer. I was behind my drums. I was with the Army Service Force Charlie Shavers's band, had a big band, playing troops off, playing them back off the ships and boats when they hit New York, down there at the piers
many a night, many a night.

And after I got out of the Army, in the meantime, Lunceford they wouldn't let nobody in Lunceford's band -- join Musician's Local #802. They were trying to break it up. And a colored guy was behind it, Peekaboo. And so, when I got out of the Army, by chance I went to the Union #802, and I ran into Mary Lou Williams, who I knew well in Memphis. And she asked me what was I doing. I says, darling, I'm not doing anything. I'm just -- I just got discharged from the Army. She say, you want a job? I say, oh, God; thank you. I certainly do. I need one.

May be going a little ahead of you, but this was 1945, when I -- I got out of the Army in 1941 five. I went in in '43. So she said, all right. Ponder me (Inaudible). She said, come down to Cafe Society --that's when it was uptown -- and talk with Ed Hall, clarinetist (Inaudible). So, boy, I was afraid because I never played with nothing but big bands, you know, like Lunceford's. And I used to go down there every night, peek -- find me a crack -- I used to peek through at the drummer and see what he was doing and how he was cutting it.

But Mary Lou Williams for some reason couldn't stand (Arthur) Trappier this fellow. Shapiro was his name. And so she had me to come and speak to Ed Hall. Sure enough, I did, and so I got a job there, did all right, did quite well. I'm very proud of myself. Perseverance is a great thing. When you're hungry --

oh, you -- I was with that little girl there, my wife, [Irene] Crawford. I used to go down there every night and peek through that crack, standing on the outside, looking in, cold, wet, rain, anything. I just wanted to see what the drummer was doing. He was cutting a show, fast hands.

So I got in Cafe Society with Ed Hall, stayed with Ed Hall for over three years. I was very good. And so they have another Cafe Society downtown, down in the Village, number 1, Sheridan Square, I think the number was. I stayed with Ed Hall for over three years, beautiful person to work for, just beautiful.

And I was living at 513 Edgecombe. That's there at 159 150th and 9th and Edgecombe with that little lady there. So I finally started to playing those Broadway musicals and making records with everybody, records on top of records, Jackie Gleason, Ethel Merman, Carol Channing, Carol Bruce.
(Inaudible).
Well, I tell you what. You go ahead, and when you get to the end, then we'll go back.
I'm getting [out].
Okay.
Then I finally saved up enough money, Stanley, and bought this mausoleum here.
(Laughter)
Twelve or 14 rooms around in here somewhere. Bought it, and

I paid for it in two years. I didn't want to pay no notes and interest and all that. We paid it off in two years. And so here I am (Inaudible) right now, very happy; at least I accomplished something out of all I did in the music business, started out with nothing, wound up with this, car in the garage, which is snowbound. So I did something, and I'm very proud of old Jimmy Crawford.
I'm very arrogant and egotistical and I don't know what all you call me. But when I'm with you, I'm going to stay with you, be with you all the way through. [Stick it out until] the end.
(Inaudible).

Oh, yeah, the pianist, Billy Kyle. He was rehearsing a show downtown by the name of "Alive and Kicking," I think, and they wanted a drummer, colored drummer supposed to be a swing drummer, because when you're in the pits, you have no reason to be flashy, like in a Broadway musical.
So I went in that show, and I played over 21 Broadway musicals. They really set me up. You know, I told you about that.
Well, I tell you now, what I'd like to do is go back to, now we've got -- now we see --
Would you like another cup?
Yeah, another cup of coffee would be
all right.
All right.
That okay with you?
Certainly.

All right. Now, what I'd like to do is go back to Booker Washington and your -- how you -- see, now we know -- now, see, we know that we've got a -- I want to deal with your childhood. See, all this stuff that you've explained in general, we want to fill all those --
Spots in --
-- spots in, you know, with more details.

Well, the only thing I can say about that Booker Washington, that was -- just happened to be his name. And he was the most sensational drummer I ever saw. I've seen Chick Webb. I've seen Buddy Rich, which is a fast -- he's fast as lightning. Chick Webb, without a doubt, was one of the greatest drummers that ever lived, hunchback Chick Webb. Now, I'm trying to see what --
Well, this is more what I wanted to do, like now, where did you get your first -- first drum set or your first drums?
Well, the school I was going to, Stanley, they didn't have a drum set. So I just went out and worked. You know, I picked cotton when I was a kid, worked at

the cotton fields, I worked at a grocery store, delivering groceries, 30 cents a day, and on Saturdays I made 60 cents. So I just saved up hoping that I could. I'd give my grandmother, my grandparents what little change I could gather, press clothes, clean clothes with a brush, you know, scrub it, and odds and ends around the neighborhood, stack balls in a poolroom. You know, man, I did all kind of work just to try to go ahead. Now, anything else you'd like to ask me...
Yeah, now, like your first -- now, you -- one thing you -- now, you said at the school you went to they didn't have any drums.

No, they had -- I started out as a peck horn player. A peck horn, you know what that is? A peck horn is an English horn and straight up, you know, like a baritone, an old tuba. I started out as a peck horn.
So now, when you started playing the drums --
The drums?
Thank you. When you started playing the drums, how -- what did you (inaudible)?
I didn't have no formal education on drums. I didn't have a teacher or nothing. I just sat behind them and just started to banging on them in Lunsford's band.
Well, during high school?
During high school, Lakeside, Ohio,
Cleveland, Buffalo, on the territory run in that vicinity.
So did you -- what kind of things did you have to play in those days? Did you have to play --
Just regular -- just try to play swing and jazz drums.
Now, did you -- what I'm saying is like did you -- how did you learn --
To play music?
Play like you roll -- different rolls and --
Rolls?
-- and different kinds of beats?

I guess I was a natural. I finally heard -- I'm jumping a little bit. I finally heard Cozy Cole playing a solo known as Ratamacue. That's what it sounded like, Ratamacue. And Paradiddles is the name of it, paradiddle, paradiddle. In other words, paradiddle, paradiddle, see how my hands are going? Right, left, right, right, left, left, so on. So I asked Cozie, I said, how do you execute that? So he told me. It's in there in the book. I said, what book?
And I got this book that I learned how to do my ratamakes and the paradiddles. Rolls, I always had some kind of rolls. And I did that. And so --
So now, what year is this that we've
been --
When I did what?
When you talked -- when you talked to him about the drums.
Oh, just when he was with either Callaway Caraway or one of the other bands, we put out a record on paradiddles.
Yeah, I have that record.

Yeah. He said, this is the most swinging rudiment to me of all of them, ratamakes and all the five stroke rolls, seven stroke rolls, said the paradiddle is the most swinging, Craw. They called me Craw back in those days and still do. May I smoke?
Yeah, oh, sure.
Will you have one?
No, thank you. So like -- so now, when you started playing -- what I mean is like, when you -- when you started playing with Luceford Tunsford's band in high school --
I didn't have no musical knowledge of drumming or just on what I could see from other drummers and pick up. Oh, yes, I was a stealer.
(Laughter)
It had to be because I didn't have no education on drums, and I enjoyed my -- I enjoy my drums. I love my drums. I certainly do. I have a set sitting in the sun parlor now,

sits there. We put it out there. I didn't want to put it on my clean rugs. You know, you never know what happens. I have -- have them sitting up in here most of the time. I've got about three or four outfits out there in the garage, in the basement. Yeah, I love my drums.
So now, what -- now, when you started playing in high school, what kinds of beats did you have to play? I mean would you -- were you --
Four-four (Inaudible) up on a bass drum, up on a snare drum? We used to -- have a little lick, we used to roll like on it. S-s-sh-ump-s-s-sh-ump, and then we used a cymbal.
(Inaudible). How about Sy Oliver?
What about it?
Oh, we're going to get to him. I know about him. Now, you say you were playing -- say you would be playing four quarter notes on the bass drum?
Yeah.
You were playing four quarter notes on the bass drum? And you would be playing --
Snare drum.
-- like press roll.
Press roll, that's it. You're right. You're a drummer.
Yeah.
Yeah. And then finally we went to the cymbal up on the stands.
Now, did you -- during those years did you ever get a chance to hear either on record or in person Zutty Singleton or --
Oh, yeah, I knew Zutty well.
And -- where'd you meet him? Did you meet him before you got to New York?
I met Zutty, to be frank with -- no, I met Zutty here in New York.
You met him in New York. Did you know Baby Dodds?
I didn't know Baby Dodds, but I heard so much about him from New Orleans. Yes, I knew of Baby Dodds. They tell me -- Dobbs, it is -- what --
It's Dodds.
Dodds, Capital D-o-d-g-s?
Yeah, right.
I knew of him. He was supposed to be during his heyday the most sensational drummer in New Orleans (inaudible). Oh, he was playing with King Louis Armstrong's (inaudible) King Oliver and all them.
Now, did you hear -- now, when you were like a kid in Memphis, did you hear -- did any of these guys come through Memphis and you get a chance to hear them, like
King
Gene Oliver or --
No.
-- or Jerry Roll... (incredible)
They may have come through there, but I didn't hear them. I didn't have the money to go hear them.
Uh-huh.
Godley
I see Alphonso Trent with A. G. Gardner on drums, who was a sensation.
Right.

And all bands like that played with territories, Zack White, Helvey's band, but my -- the most impressive band I ever heard was Alphonso Trent out of Little Rock. Oh, man, he had a good little band. And --
What was it you liked about the band?
Their swing, their style and their excitement. And Snub Moseley was with that band then.
Yeah, you had --
And Stuff Smith also.
Stuff Smith was with them.
Yeah.
Now, was he -- he was playing -- was he playing -- he was playing violin.
Yeah.
Was he -- now, they didn't have any
microphones. They didn't -- he didn't use a microphone, did he?
No, I don't think so. I don't remember, but they didn't use no microphone.
Did they feature him on slow pieces or fast pieces or both? Do you remember?
Well, medium, slow. I don't remember. A. G. Gardner on those drums. Boy, that man really was a sensation to me.
What was it that he played that you liked?
Just the way he played, period. He was ahead of time. Like he played the northern type of drumming.
Now, when you say the northern type of drumming, (solo and (inaudible)), cymbals --
I got that thing from him on the cymbals.
You mean the playing with the side cymbals?

(inaudible) beat on the top ride cymbal, dump-tickatee-dump-tickatee-dump- toclatee-dump, with that left hand going underneath there with the stick underneath it. I can do that very well. It's still in me, twirling the sticks I got from Booker Washington. Oh, thatman was something
else.
Some --

Looked like wheels on his fingers. Throwing them in there, catching them in here, horns, big (inaudible) automobile horns like they used to use on those Packards and whatnot, shooting blank pistols. He did everything.
Now, he would --
(Laughter)
-- so you mean now he would be playing, and he would be throwing the sticks in the air.
Yeah, and some still coming out on the snaredrum or on the bass drum. He would throw them in there and grab it, keep playing, but something was always going on on the drums. I couldn't understand it.
And he had squeeze horns?
Everything -- squeeze horns, pistols, blanks. He's playing. You hear a pistol go off. You jump.
(Laughter)
And he did -- he did the most amazing things I ever saw.
So now, did he -- what kind of a setup did he have? Did he use a --
A lot of gadgets around these drums. He could squeeze and shoot and all of that, just a regular outfit.
Uh-huh. Like he'd snaredrum. Were they using the sock cymbal then?
Yes. You know what kind of sock cymbal it was? Flat on the floor.
The short one, about -- what about 12 --
Yeah, that's it.
-- inches off the floor?
Yeah.
Okay. Now, do you remember when -- oh, since we're on the subject of sock cymbal --
Kaiser Marshall, to me, first one I saw play a high hat cymbal.
Uh-huh.
Pardon me just a minute. I got to go to the --
[PAUSE]
All right. I'll turn this -- I'll turn it off. Right, now --
High hat.
Right, we were talking about the high hat. You said the first tall -- high hat you saw was Kaiser Marshall was playing.
Yeah, he could play it too. He could do that stuff underneath that stick, all that.
Huh. What y ear was this? Do you
remember what year this was in, roughly?
Well, I think he brought them out. I, you know, I think he brought them out, high hat cymbal.
Now, you say that -- you say there was a -- now, you were saying earlier that there -- excuse me (there was) (inaudible) what you call a northern style and a southern style of drumming.
Well, it's --
Well, there was the northern. You used the term northern style.
Yeah.
What would you term southern style?

Well, south ern style was strictly snare drum, choke cymbal, that sh-sh-chum-sh-sh-sh-sh, sh-sh-- chum, sh-sh-sh-h-h, you know, that style and snare drum. Northern style -- played more freely. Joe Jones (inaudible) was really -- he revolutionized the drums to me. He played so freely with Basie and smooth as silk. Occasionally, pardon me, (the Club Harlem) Basie would call me over. I was playing a club, played there for many summers.

And Basie, whenever Joe decided to play sick, wouldn't show up or something like that, Basie needed a drummer. So they had two drummers over at the Club Harlem. I didn't play no dance music. I strictly played the shows, which were about an hour or two long. I played the shows, so I went over and
played in Joe's place, subbed for him.
This was in the late '30s?
I don't know what year it was. It was later than that. What I mean, in the '40s, wasn't it?
(Inaudible).
I told him about Cafe Society.
Yeah, but go ahead. Now, but what were you saying about the northern style. You were saying that -- now, what was it that you -- that Joe Jones did -- to use the northern style?

Oh, Joe Jones revolutionized the new trend of drumming, freely, that silk style, (inaudible) the cymbal up here, brushes or sticks, and he played some tremendous breaks. I have a record here now about Basie, featuring Joe Jones. Old Man River -- Old Man -- let me see. He'd get in a part tempo, way up. He'd get in one part of that solo, and he started to playing it with his bass drum 4-4. Toogaloo-loo-loo-loo. And he had -- he just could play it to me.
Now, now, let's go back again to --
(Inaudible).
Right. We got a lot of material to go over.
(Laughter)
Now, we -- now, when --
You look like Fred Norman.
Oh, do I?
Anybody ever tell you that?
No.
(Inaudible).

Oh, we're going to get to that. But I wanted to get back to the high school part. Now, when you were playing -- so you say, when -- you just picked up playing -- you picked up, when you were in high school and Luncaford came back, and you were with his band in high school, right?
That's where I started out.
Uh-huh. Now, were you -- did you practice the drums a lot then or did you --
No.
You didn't practice them. You just --
No.

Didn't know what to practice, just get on the jobs and play what came to my mind. Of course, I had to coincide. I had to fit in with what they were playing. No, I didn't practice.

Well, that I didn't know, but I think they knew that he was colored. But he didn't look it. He was white as Dorsey. What I mean, not hairstyle, because he had always black hair. Good hair, like Cab Calloway. And after Willie, Wilcox, pianist. Wilcox was always a tight man. By that I mean he wasn't a spendthrift. He'd hold on to a dime or a nickel as long as he could. He wouldn't spend on nobody, like, buy a drink for some [broad,] no. He was a tight man. Yeah. Great trombone player. And a lot of guys right today, Trummy practiced blowing in a pop bottle with a straw. He said Dorsey told him to do that in order to get that circular --
Breathing.

Breathing. Yeah, Trummy used to stand around, blowing in that bottle. I used to look at him, I wasn't too down with anybody that always applied themselves too religiously about practicing. Me, I wasn't practicing, that's why I was a dumb -- I was a good player, but I didn't -- practice? No. That's why I'm going to get on my single strokes, get my fingers fast.

I don't play now, but in case I do get a call for a job or a show, I'll take it. "Oh, man, this is too good." And Ernie told a lie, talking about -- he's not in the band, he was one of them, writer talking about they were paying him four doubles. Four doubles, and he only played a trumpet.

I'm the one that was getting the doubles, because I was playing drums, tympany, whatnot, even though they had the percussionists in there. But I'd have to go over sometime and hit a note. If I hit one, got to pay me. I wouldn't take that show unless they paid me well, with two doubles at the most -- I mean, at the least. Two doubles you got to give me, on top of my union salary. Yes, sir. I wouldn't take a Broadway show.
[Ernie Lawrence] spoiled me. Didn't I tell you about me marching in the march on Washington, with --
Oh, yeah, you mentioned that, but we're going to get to that just a little bit later.
Yeah, we got to fill this thing out here.

Yeah. Now, I was going to say, now, Sy Oliver, we didn't talk about Sy Oliver. Now, do you -- I wanted to ask you something. There's some argument that goes on between different people about where the style of the Lunceford band came from. Some people say it came from Sy Oliver.
That's right. We had other arrangers
in there, such as Roger Seguerie and people like that. They were ofay boys. But Sy Oliver, technically speaking, contributed -- you going to read or listen?
No, I'm listening

He contributed more to the Lunceford style than anybody. We didn't have no style prior to Sy Oliver joining the band. But when Sy got there, he made sure you played his arrangements the way he wanted them. And -- which was a great thing. He contributed a great deal to that band.

No, it was simple, but it had to be right, though. Sy wrote simply, even the things he went over there and did with Tommy Dorsey, when he started writing for Dorsey, after he left the band. Sy wrote simple, but he wrote with a beat. That bum could really write.

I mean, he was self-educated. He never had a lesson in arranging in his life. He just -- people had a piano, so he sat down and taught himself how to arrange. He was a pretty brilliant, bigheaded guy.
Well, how did he -- being as good a musician as he was, being paid as poorly as he was being paid, but Lunceford, how did he react to that?
Well, he still wanted to go out there

and throw some dirt on Lunceford's grave in his face. Due to the fact that he knew he was getting so underpaid, he was being underpaid so badly. You couldn't change Lunceford's, Oxley's mind. Oh, man, don't let me get started talking about him myself. Because -- is this on?
Yeah, go ahead.

Because after all the time that I spent in that band, I used to see Dutch Williams, who was the road manager -- getting a little tired now, but I'm going to finish this. Come by every night after the job in the bus, and would give Lunceford some money.

Well, later on -- Mose Allen discovered it, bass player -- that Lunceford was a hired man, just like we were in the band. Now, Lunceford's dead, Oxley's dead, but I can say it, and I'm saying it. He was hired just like we were. And yet, Lunceford was the owner and the leader of the band. Only he was getting very paid every night and we got paid every week.
Was this before or after Irving Mills got involved with this band?
This was after.
Do you think Irving Mills was involved in the band being taken over like that?
Well, I don't know, but you bet your life Oxley got his training from somebody, because

Lunceford was getting -- I don't know how much he was getting, but Dutch Williams would come by every night in that bus after we finished a gig, on his way up to the front of the bus to talk with the driver, but he'd always stop at Lunceford's seat which was the second or the first seat.
Well, with all of the travelling and playing these one-nighters and having to sleep on the bus and all of this, how did you all keep up the energy to --
Morale and energy?
Yeah, how did you keep that up to play?

Well, I'll tell you what, Stanley. Everybody that played in that band had their hearts and souls in it. All those that didn't, they knew they were in the wrong place. They had to go somewhere else. You just don't come in Lunceford's band and figure that you're going to run yourself and do what you want to do, no, not in Lunceford's band. Yet, we were happy all the time. We did what Lunceford wanted us to do, because he was a leader of men. Pardon me.

Yeah, you know what I'm saying, in terms of -- like, because, like, if you're playing those one-nighters, there's a lot of, like, time when you don't sleep too well or something and you got to play. How many hours did you all used to have to play a night, if you were playing? How many sets did you play?
Four.
You played four hours?
Yeah, from 8:30 or 9:00 until 2:00 in the morning. Four or five hours. That was -- all bands had to play, mostly.
And you said the band was a very exciting band, too, you said the guys --
Oh, yeah. They put on a show for them.
Did you all work that out before you went out to play?
No, things just going, things just started happening. Trumpeters would throw their trumpets in the air, all at the same time, simultaneously. Is this on?
Yeah.
And they'd catch them. And they would change mutes at the same time. Everything was precise.
And these things were spontaneous. They happened on the bandstand.
Spontaneous, spontaneous. Eddie Durham brought a trick in there, where you throw your trombone and all of a sudden you just let it go, and slide --
And the slide comes off?
Almost off, but for some reason, he had the knack of catching it and his hands was back here, right-handed or left-handed, and would catch it just before it would

fall. So we had the trombones doing that. Saxophones -- well, they used to promenade around, in and out of the wings, in and out of the bandstand, blowing, still blowing. Just the rhythm stayed on the stage.
We had a glee club that really sang.
Oh, that's right because you all did those choral arrangements, too, that were in the band.
Yes, sir. Sy Oliver started that. He was very much an instigator, and shaping that band. That's all I got to say about him.

Yeah, well, I think that had a -- because I know I've heard Ellington recording in which it seems as though they had heard -- Duke had heard that, there was a record called 'I Just Got To Be A Rug Cutter.' And Harry Carney and a couple of the other guys in the band are singing harmony.

Yeah, well, they got it from us. I won't say that's a true statement, but they were inspired by that Lunceford band. Man, we put on a show. And it was done simultaneously, just automatically created while he were playing. Now, we did rehearse the choral group, oh, yes, had to rehearse that. That was like playing.
I'm getting a little tired, now.
Let me turn this off.

Yes.

Elaborate a little bit on it.
Yeah.

I would love to. You know, I laid off from listening to the band, and I hear all this avant garde guys. But that Lunceford band, without a doubt, bar none, was the cleanest band I've heard of all of them. And I got so engrossed in it the other day, when my wife was playing it for me, until I just -- every number she played was so clean, so precise, that reed section, you couldn't beat them. That includes Duke's section and all the rest of them. Rhythm section, yeah, you had better drummers, better bass players, perhaps, but when it came down to the rhythm section, they were just in there. Maybe a little heavy at times, maybe a little punctuated too much, but all in all, that whole entire band was so precise. I enjoyed it.
How did you all get the kind of discipline that it took for that kind of cleanness to come out of the band?

whatnot. But I have to give credit where it's due. That Sy Oliver got in there and Willie Smith, yes, he arranged. But all of them had to just take their hats off to Sy Oliver. If you didn't do it right. But Willie Smith, without a doubt, would get very horrified with any saxophone player there -- Jack Carruthers, Joe Thomas, Willie Smith, any of them in that band. Now, if you want me to conduct? Tell these fellows that they have to play the way I'm playing. Oh, he was the living end (inaudible) and all of them popping right together. And Lunceford, so clean, dible), the question you asked me, Lunceford was the one that established discipline in that band.
Do you think it had anything to do with his educational background, with him having --

Without a doubt. The man was a leader. Duke Ellington was a leader, but not the type that Lunceford was. That's why they wanted to break that band up when we first hit New York. They wouldn't let us in the union. Finally got in there, I mean, I did, and all the guys that couldn't cut it the way it was supposed to be cut, they fell by the wayside, Stanley.
What were the requirements for getting in the union in those days?

Well, I don't know what the joining fee was, I've forgotten. But the requirement -- we were union men, but we were unionized in Buffalo, New York. 533, that was the number of that local in Buffalo. But to get in 802, which is the New York musician's union, well, you just had to either quit the band -- that's it, quit the band and join the union. They wouldn't let us in that union unless we had quit the band. I had to quit, because when Uncle Sam reached out for World War II, I went in the army to play drums, not to carry a gun and to go over and shoot and kill.

So I played two years in the Army Service force band at Camp Kilmer, right over here in Jersey. Yes, that's all I did, played drums. Military drums, man, I can see right now. I'm practicing marches, such as Semper Fidelis, and various marches. You had to play the troops over on the boats, of course, we did, we played them right to the gangplank, and turned around and went back to camp. And then we met them as they came back from the war and play them off the boats. That was my duty. Playing with this large Army Service force band.

And so, I don't know what happened to most of the fellows. Joe Turner, piano player, he played bass (inaudible) in the band, and people like that. He's in Europe somewhere, Belgium or somewhere. The other guys was scattered about, some

of them gone, some of them died, but the remainder, I didn't keep in touch with them, much. Not that I didn't want to, but I was just in my thing. I had to go make a living and a name for Jimmy Crawford. And that's what I did to the best of my ability. I went through hell, man, I went -- and I know I know a lot, and I have a lot of experiences that I witnessed. My memoirs are treasurable. I just -- I'm proud of knowing what I know about travelling from Maine to Florida, New York to California, and halfway around the world, Scandinavia, India, Great Britain, France. I didn't play in Italy, but I went through there just to find out what was happening.
How did you like it?

Wonderful. Only thing, I wasn't involved or interested in women, as most bandsmen do. All I wanted to do was to hear music, and I got some bands in my mind, Speed Webb, which I first heard Roy Eldridge. I don't know where Speed was from, I think around -- well, anyway, out in the Middle West or somewhere, Indiana or somewhere. McKinney's Kenny's Cotton Pickers, Zack White, Helvey's band. Oh, they were the swingingest bands in the land. Alphonso Alphonso Trent --
How did you end up going through Italy?
Well, the band was in Europe.
The Lunceford band?
Yeah, the Lunceford band, and we was just travelling, hoping for a gig. And so we went down to
Italy. First we went to Scandinavia -- Stockholm, Norway, Sweden, all the important cities there, that could afford to hear this band. I'm very proud of that band.
And you played in Great Britain, too.
I guess so. It's hard for me to remember. But I was there, in London. Principal city in Great Britain, just to hear and listen and learn.
What kind of music were they playing in London when you came there?

Well, something copied after the Americans. They had colored guys, white fellows. Benny Goodman, King of Swing, so they say. He was a great clarinettist but to me, nobody outswung Basie, Count Basie. Or Lips Page.
Did you ever play with Hot Lips Page?
Yes, many times. Hot Lips Page. His former wife just died. Not too long ago.
What kind of a man did you find Page?

Beautiful. That man, you know what he used to do, Stan? Like, he'd see me sitting across the street from the hotel, on a stoop, old concrete stoop, legs stretched out on the sidewalk. You know, Lips would make it a point to come by and sit and talk with me and give me advice, and tell me the things to do, and he was just so jovial, and I'd listen. Oh, he and I would have the greatest conversations. He did that for most all bands. Come by and sit and

talk with them, on the street, on the sidewalk, on the curb, didn't make no difference. He was a beautiful man. There was a man by my house two or three days ago by the name of Arthur [Aarons]. He married Hot Lips' former wife, Elizabeth. And she passed here not too long ago, during last summer, somewhere around in there. And she told him, told her husband, who was Arthur [Hines], everything that she wanted done to her body. She said, I know I'm going to die and it's going to be soon. She had cancer of the throat. She said, I know I'm going to die, but I want you to promise me that you're going to do this, Arthur. I want my body cremated, put in ashes, and set them up, not on display, but like, on a mantel or -- just keep them.

So he did. She told him, say, you got to promise me, said, because I know I'm going to die. I don't want my body laying in the casket, in the ground, termites chewing me up and all that. I want to be cremated. So he did it. And so, here come this sister, the girl Elizabeth's sister -- I'm talking about Hot Lips' Page ex-wife. They were together, and so Elizabeth's sister came up and got on Arthur Hines to cremate her body, having it burn up into ashes. I mean, he caught the devil from her. Elizabeth's sister.
And so, what happened, came up here from somewhere in the South, but he had it done. She made him promise.
Tell me this, concerning Page. What kind of advice would he give you, do you recall any of that?
Yeah, just -- the man would just talk in general about music-wise, musicianship. (Yes). He had good experience.
Did he encourage you to learn how to read, those kind of things?
Oh, yeah. Got to read, or else I wouldn't have been playing those 20 -- over 20 Broadway musicals. I'm very proud of that, had to read.
Which bands -- can you recall some of the -- like, say, when you all got to New York, didn't you recall who some of the best readers, in terms of the bands around were, or individual musicians?

I didn't look at it from that standpoint. The best readers -- you had to read, because in all those bands, Duke Ellington, Chick Webb, oh, you got just many bands. A lot of them played by head, head arrangements. But when a guy would bring his arrangements in there, you got to cut it.
Yeah, you have to cut that.
Did Sy ever write out drum parts for you?

Oh, yeah. Mostly, he relied on my ability to listen along with the arrangement. I had a part, oh, yes, I had a drum part. But drumming -- drum music is just really on one line, well, two, with the bass drum and your

snare drum. But he had cymbals in there -- what I mean by cymbals, to denote P, which is piano, double-P is double piano, soft and soft and triple and so on. And your F's are forte. We call it forte, but it's still forte. And all that, yeah, he had the cymbal there. And he would -- ups and downs --
Did he have the parts written in notes or did he just describe -- have a description down there for you?
Well, in drum notes, we just played C's and -- for your top, that's snare drum.
Did you tune your snare drum? (Unintelligible)

No, I didn't tune no drums. Jo Jones say he does. I just play on them, get up on them and play them. When they finally get through sitting up there, I'd get up there and play them. I didn't have no tuning device. Well, I could them actually, with a drum key. But I enjoyed playing arrangements, no head stuff. We had a few head numbers in there, which were very good. But arrangements is what I enjoyed, beautiful arrangements -- big ones, good ones, symphonics, so-called, because we weren't no symphony men.
But when you cut an arranger's arrangements, you never know what you're confronted with.
Did you all ever in those days, say, in the '30s, when you all got to New York and began to make a name for the band, did you all encounter many symphony musi-

That I don't know, because you never know who's in the audience. You never know who's around. Some fellows had symphonic training, but they couldn't make it in swing bands. I'm talking mainly of whites. They couldn't make it. Swinging is a natural thing. You can't play the blues, you're in trouble. The blues will tell you off, in other words. In other words, show you up. If you can't cut the blues, that includes drummers and everybody else. They don't know how to play the blues, shame on you. Case is closed, yes, sir.
But, now, you were saying to me earlier that -- when you started playing the drums, that you didn't really know anything about the drums.
No, I really didn't.
How did you learn to read?

I taught myself. Take a little drink of apple cider, you all. What I'm trying to say is, I taught myself, just like I'm sitting here now, starting at the beginning of a book, when I find I've got enough sense in my head. I got a lot of books here on drums, to sit and practice on. Do it slow, that's the way I did it. And learn. I didn't have no musical education.
About what time in your career did you begin studying out of books?
When I went into Broadway musicals, back in 19 -- I don't know, well, I got in in 1939 or somewhere around in there.
Oh, you were playing --
I was playing drums, and --
You were playing in musicals before you left the Lunceford -- you left the Lunceford band in '42, didn't you?
Yeah, but I was starting in -- well, I left when the Army grabbed me. That's when I started to playing --
Marches and stuff, with the band, in the army

Yeah, and I started playing Broadway musicals when I came out. No, wait a minute, now, I really can't remember that. Aline, do you know when I started playing musicals? I got it in my wallet. I have it in my wallet, right back there, all the shows I ever did. It's 19 -- I think, yeah, -- oh, no.
(inaudible) 1950.
Look in my wallet. Pardon me a minute.
Well, now, if you started learning to read --
That's [why when] I started to study.
Yeah.
For 'Alive and Kicking,' which was your first --
Yeah.
-- musical. But, now, you said a little earlier that you had been reading (drum) parts that --
(Unintelligible.)
But, now, that's what I was trying to find out a little bit earlier, when you were saying that Sy Oliver had parts for you.
Yeah.
Did he tell you what he wanted you to play, or did he write down --
Oh, he wrote it down.
He wrote it down on music paper.

Wrote it down, because Sy Oliver was a staunch believer in playing what he wanted to play. Phrasing-wise and playing. Now, he would write me a drum part, and everybody in that band, he would write it. That's what he wanted you to play.

That was a guide, like, a guide sheet. Music is nothing for drums but mathematics, adding and subtraction, and all that kind of -- that's all, just straight time, and then if he wants you to accent something, then he'd put a mark over it, where you knew what to do. Catch this and that, write it,

verbally and musically. And then when I first started to realizing that I really had to read, no more going by ear, which I was great at that. That's why I say, you got to know how to play the blues. Then you can get a lot of education from the blues.
And then I started studying.
Now, when you say you can get a lot of education from the blues, what do you mean?

Well, if you got it musically, it will show up, if you can play the blues. Wire brushes, sticks, things like that. If you can't the blues, then you might as well forget it and go try to get in the longhair company. Then you have to go to great musical schools and all of that, and get acquainted with that, and start playing in the schools' orchestras. In other words, get your training. You got to start all over again.

Blues, you get your longhair come in a band going to sit there and try to fake a blues solo or something, he doesn't fit. Doesn't fit. Now, Tommy Dorsey can do it, but he still bash'n't got that spook in there. I mean, that down home, old fashioned blues, which is ignorant music to me. I don't want to hear no Ma Rainey Maurania and all that bunch. I want to hear somebody, when they sing the blues, sing the blues.
Well, who were some of your favorite blues singers, as long as we're on the subject?

My favorite blues singers? Well, the ones that came to the Palace Theatre in Memphis, when my aunt would take me. Ma Rainey, back in those days, Bessie Smith -- I read Bessie Smith had a gigantic sound as a singer.

Oh, yeah. Bessie Smith, Ida Cox, Baby Cox and all -- Bessie Smith, oh, yeah, she was a blues stomper. Those were the original blues singers. And on and off, Bessie was one of the tops. Ida Cox, and here there's one I heard the other night. It was on Dinah's show, Dinah Washington's show. Now, Dinah Washington can sing, also, the blues. Sarah Vaughan, she can sing the blues, but she scat too much for me. Got a nice voice, though. Billie Holiday could sing the blues.
You like the way she sang, huh?

Yes. That's a great difference in singers. I remember when they used to sit in the background or sit up front, he didn't have no voice to say anything or do anything, especially the singers, until Sinatra came along. And there were three of them, not three Sinatras, but three fellows, a trio. And Dorsey only took Sinatra. And he got out front.
Well, I was listening to something of -- one of the Lunceford numbers, and Sy Oliver was singing.
Yeah. He was --
Well, there was something I wanted to ask you, because I had heard -- well, it sounds to me -- now, see, I may have this maybe absolutely wrong --
Then ask me, I'll tell you who he was.
But, it's like -- it sounds to me sometimes as though Bing Crosby had an effect on the way guys sang in the '30s.

Well, certainly. He had an effect on Sinatra, all of them. He was before Sinatra. But as music went, the style of playing and the style of sounds like years ago, you had the honky tonk travelling music. And then it went into swing and then it went into -- I mean, it went into Dixieland, and then from Dixieland it went into swing. And then it went into bebop. And it's just changed.
Like, you were talking about singers. Now, I -- Bing Crosby had to have some kind of influence on Sinatra.
Well, do you think he had any influence on singers like Benny Carter and Sy Oliver and any of the black singers?
Yes, well, certainly, because he came along first.
Now, could you -- going back to the subject that you had about blues playing, do you recall the way that the blues beat developed for the drums?
When I was -- pardon me, Stanley, but

I was raised in a blues town, Memphis. And places like that, where the riverboats used to come through by Memphis, went through on the Mississippi River. And you had bands on there that you could stand on (the) levee, and you'd listened to those trumpets and those old slide trombones. Trumpets would be punctuating the air with blues. That's all they had in their minds, blues. Everything that they had played consisted of some kind of blues. (Singing.)

That kind of stuff. Oh, you had to have it in you. You couldn't get a symphonic (guy to come and out of) -- play that kind of stuff. Colored people, boy, they contributed more than a lot of people realized, and admit that they contributed. They did the thing, when it come to that soul music and soul food, that kind of stuff, you just can't beat them.

(Unintelligible) ofay guy, I'm not going after all that, anyway, because everybody God put on this earth and created, supposed to be the same. Some have something, -- now, you go to Africa, and come the drummers, you never in your life heard such great independence like they can do in Africa. I have not had the pleasure of going to Africa, but I've (listened) and I've learned.

You get a guy, two or three guys together, and they can make the greatest contribution to swinging and independence -- (singing), had all that going. That's a natural beat. They got the beat, but they started to throwing in triplets and all
with their left hand and left foot and all that. I can do that. I had to study and study hard on it, though.

In other words, for independence. Piano players have to have independence. Their left hand is doing one thing and their right hand is doing another, and organ players, they got to contend with that foot down there. On those pedals. Piano players had to have independence.
Well, now, when they were playing -- when you heard the bands on the riverboats playing blues, what were the drummers playing? Were they playing mostly like press rolls and --
Yeah, uh-huh. And that (singing), you know, on the cymbals. But the blues are slow, and you can play up-tempo blues, also. Basie's got a blues band.
Let me turn this tape over. It looks like we've gotten to the end. It looks like we've gotten to the end of this side.
All right.
We're getting closer to the --
I want to do that, The sooner the better, (Unintelligible)
Okay.
(End of Side One.)
-- that you heard playing on --
Press rolls.
Press rolls.
Yeah, the trumpets were sticking those high notes [in,] and that blues sound. Oh, the trombones were sliding --
Were they using plungers much then, the trumpet players?

Yeah, Bubber Miley was the man that was a genius at that. People give Cootie Williams credit, but Cootie apparently got it from Bubber Miley. Down from New Orleans, down from the South somewhere. Those guys had natural ability. I don't know about his reading ability, but bet your life they knew that instrument they were playing. Now, --
So, now, they were playing press rolls on the snare drum. Were they playing it on the bass drum, too?
Yeah.
This is like when you were a kid [wasn't it?]
Oh, yeah, they played --
Because you were born in 1910, you were, like, what, we're talking about 19, '18, '19, '20?
Yeah, around World War I.
And what were they playing on the bass drum, were they playing, like, --
Four-four. They didn't have the technique (Unintelligible) modern drum have, but they

were playing. That's where we got our beginnings on, press rolls and bass drum, wood blocks, things like that. Yeah, that was back as early as I can remember, around about World War I. I wasn't playing no drums then.

Well, why do you think drummers stopped using, like, the temple blocks and the triangles and -- like, I've known photographs of drummers in the late 20s and early '30s, they have temple blocks, they got triangles, gong over here, they got --
Ratchets.
Ratchets, right.
Yeah.
Did they have all those things because of them playing, like, in shows? I mean, like, in music houses where they'd have to have effects for movies?

Yeah, yeah. And then Sonny Greer, you know, came along and upset the whole thing by having a whole complete set of drums around him, in other words, around him, such as drum outfit, temple blocks, ratchets. I don't know whether he had ratchets, maybe he didn't, but he had wood blocks, chimes, gongs, cymbals, an array of cymbals. Boy, but that Buddy Rich, nobody could touch that man, including Chick Webb.
That man is absolutely, without a doubt, bar none, to me, the greatest snare drum player that I ever saw.
Including symphony players? Does he play --

Yeah, including any of them. Symphony players, concert players, don't mention them. Throw them out of your mind. Buddy Rich, without a doubt, is the greatest snare drum player, to me, that ever lived. And he taught himself. Every time a man get those single strokes down, it's easy to do Mama-Daddy. That's double strokes. But single strokes, to me, is the foundation of all good drummers. All good drummers.
So, I can call the names and all, but thinking of them offhand is pretty hard for me. O'Neill Old Needie Spencer was another good one.
Who were some of your favorite bass players that you liked to play with?

Well, Milt Hinton, number one. And Oscar Pettiford. Of course, he was playing a bass like a violin player. But, I mean, he was just great execution-wise. And then you had -- oh, so many good bass players. But you still could put them on -- count them on your hands, on your fingers. Milt Hinton, oh, man.
What about Jimmy Blanton? What did you think of him?
Loved him. Beautiful, wonderful. He's a Big professional im there, now Oh, yeah, Jimmy
Blanton. He would have been with Duke. I don't know how Duke came about getting all great men like Jimmy Blanton, Otto Hardwick (unintelligible), Johnny Hodges, even Sonny Greer.
Tricky Sam --

Tricky Sam and those kind of people. That man has some of the greatest jazz musicians that I ever knew, and I knew them all, well, very well. Back to Lips Page. I don't know whether Lips played with Duke. I know Basie played with him, and he played with Benny Morton. That's where Basie -- Basie was a piano player, and -- just a piano player in Benny Morton's band. He took over when Morton died. And then same one of the greatest swing bands in the land.]
Now, what else?
What did you think of -- how did you like John Kirby? Did you ever play with him?
Well, not too much. Because, -- he was a good bass player, that was a good bass player.
Well, sometimes it seems to me that his small group seems to have been very influenced by the Lunceford band.
Oh, yeah.
Some of the arrangements -- I was listening to them not too long ago, it seemed like he --
Well, that was the Greatest Little

Band in the land." Yes, that band -- and McKinney's Cotton Pickers, back in Detroit. Now, how did he assemble all those great musicians in his band? Fathead on alto, even got Don Redman in there. We used to call him the Little Giant. Yeah, Little Giant. And he had -- and I don't know what instrument McKinney played. I think he was formerly a drummer, but he had a great, sensational drummer in there -- Cubie Austin. Great press roll man. Yes, McKinney you didn't see, hardly ever. He was just the boss. But -- he was just the boss of the band, McKinney's Cotton Pickers.
You were talking about the brushes earlier. When did you start -- were you playing brushes when you started playing?
No.
When did you --
I don't remember.
Did you start playing them before you left the Lunceford band?
Oh, yeah, oh, yes, oh, yes. Brushes -- play waltzes, mostly, with brushes. Stuff like that, tedious things. And on the drums, played sticks.
Well, now, who were your favorite brush men?
Pardon me a minute, I was taking a little apple cider. Big Sid Catlett. Big Sid Catlett, only
Jo Jones got most of his stuff. Oh, Sid was a very touchy fellow. Oh, he played beautiful drums. Big hands, big feet, sure could play some good drums.
Was he using the figure eight?
Yeah.
He was using the figure eight?
Yeah, that left hand was always sweeping. And then he could take solos in person. Oh, yeah, he was unlimited.
Was he one of the first that ever played brush solos?
I think he was, just like he was playing sticks, just as clear -- clarity and everything.
He must have practiced a lot, then.

Big Sid was a natural, a natural. Had to practice, but I don't know when, because he was a bar man, frequented the bars quite a bit. But he had to practice somewhere in the beginning. Something that I didn't do.
No, we were talking about -- no, I wanted to ask you something about tempos, now. Do you -- what tempos did you find the most difficult to play?
Fast tempos, because I was always very concerned about my foot and bass drum. Left foot was all right, but that bass drum, playing fast, Tiger Rag tempos

and White Heat and all of that, oh, I was scared. Whenever you called a real fast number. Jo Jones and J.C. Heard Jesse Hertz, sitting in the Apollo Theatre, and I had an embarrassing scene when I was going on there, and all of a sudden, I'm trying to play one of those very fast tempos, because I was used to hearing that bass drum.
So J.C. Jesse was sitting up in the balcony, box seats up there, and I was (inaudible).
Put two fingers up?
Two. And so I said, thank you. I wasn't in the tune, now I'm comfortable. Oh, but those fast tempos, pretty rough on me, playing. Not only me, any drummer.
Well, you know, a lot of guys today find the slow tempos harder to play. A lot of guys can play fast today.

Oh, that's [ducks], that ain't slow tempo. But I found it just the opposite. Easy, I could play the slow tempo -- well, it was just easy for me naturally. But a fast tempo, way up there? Specially pushing a big band? When they relied on me to push it? It was tough, I mean, I had to get on my toe and could hardly play anything upstairs. Your snare drum and things like that.
I finally had to learn how to cheat [with the] cymbals.
Yeah, well, then, you were -- it's funny, once you start doing it, if you start out playing the
regular beat on the cymbals, at a fast tempo and then you change it, people still think you're playing --
That's right, it's the cheating, because that foot cymbal is hitting the back beat, and up here is easy, because your cymbal is big and -- (singing). Don't increase the tempo.
Who were some of the best tempo keepers to your mind? A lot of times, you listen to things and peices start in one temp and then --

Oh, that was so many, so many good tempo men. Cupie Austin, in McKenney's Cotton Pickers, Big Sid Catlett, Jo Jones. Fall in on some breaks, there, snare drum to a sock cymbal, tom-toms, they were good men. Kaiser Marshall was a good -- had to be good to play with Fletcher Henderson's band. Old timer, but he stuck to his style.
Do you -- did you think that Fletcher Henderson's use of a lot of different keys had an effect on what kind of writing Sy Oliver did for Fletcher's band?
Had Willie Smith -- Sy Oliver?
Yeah. I remember you were telling me earlier that you remember the time when most of the tunes were written, and most of the tunes the guys played were in keys of B flat and C.
Yeah, around in there, but Fletcher Henderson, he put them in all kind of sharps and flats. That

is why Roy Eldridge -- took him a long time to get used to that band, because he played in regular keys, B flat, E flat, C's, F's, and like that. When you go into those A flats and A sharps, all that kind of stuff, took him a long time to get with it. He admitted it, too. He said they're playing in too many keys. Yeah. Great band, Fletcher's band. Saw a lot of young drummers in here.
Did you ever meet -- speaking of composers, did you ever meet Jelly Roll Morton?
Jelly Roll Morton, band man from Kansas City?
No, from New Orleans.

Oh. No, I didn't, but I knew a lot about him. I didn't have the pleasure of meeting him. But as I said, coming up in those river boat bands, they were natural musicians, sound, color, they were just -- it was amazing to stand on that levee in Memphis, Tennessee and listen to those bands coming through Memphis, and playing, and docking those boats. Oh, yeah. Alphonso Trent.
Yeah, you mention his band a lot. You must have really liked that man.

Certainly I did. He had A.C. Godley (Sensational) Gardley on drums. Alphonso Trent. Crook was his banjo player. He didn't play guitar in that band, he played banjo. Chester Clark, first trumpet player. Oh, yeah, a fellow was

telling me -- Arthur Hines, again, that he used to go -- Crooke finally settled in New York as a super in an apartment building. Say he used to go by and they'd play cards together. Crooke, banjo player formerly with Alphonso Trent. And good banjo player, rhythm-wise. Whatever way he played on the banjo. But it was good.

I wanted to ask you, too, did -- something I forgot to ask you the first time. Like, when the guys weren't working, like, during the day or something, where did they hang out? What kind of places? Were there many musicians' hang-outs that you remember, like in the '30s and '40s, or did you -

Oh, I'll tell you -- at the Rhythm Club, 130 -- right around the corner from Lafayette Theatre. They hung out at the Braddock Bar, and Dominick's Bar. That's where they hung out. Every day they had to be there. Just for their own curiosity. That's where they hung out. Alhambra Grill, places like that.
What did they do? I mean, like, --
Just hanging out.
Just hanging out?
Yeah.
Just like --
Meeting other musicians, talking.
So, like, were they just comparing notes
Yes.
How different towns they'd been to.

Oh, yeah. See, Lunceford had the world's greatest one-nighter band. Gigs, in other words, every night a different town. I got so sick of travelling, that's why right today, I'm retired. I will never travel again, in my life. If I can keep from it.
You all were travelling by bus, mostly or --

First started out in cars, and I told you an incident that happened, about me walking a mile with my drums, after I went by a fellow's house. He was always afraid -- well, I told you that, that's all right -- about going in his garage by himself, he put me out and I'd take my drums and walk about a mile to my home, in Memphis this was.

Well, tell me this, how did you all -- the travelling experiences I've had playing, the big problem even today a lot of times is getting your clothes cleaned and stuff like that, things. I mean, given the segregation and stuff, how -- did you all have any problems with getting your -- if you tried -- [in other words, are you saying, every night like, another town?
Daily, nightly. Segregation is the

most despised word in my life, other than depression. I very seldom use those words, but segregation, we confronted that every night. When we wanted to go to a hotel, no, go to one of those cheap colored hotels. They were the only ones that would put us up.

Yeah, I know, there was one guy -- there was a guy was just telling me that there were guys -- there were some black guys in the South who took advantage of the segregation, they would overcharge musicians for --
I assume they did, but we couldn't stay in no white hotels. There was some mean people back down South then, even right here in the North, very mean people.
Like, in which areas?
Which areas?
That stand out in your mind.

Well, anywhere -- New England, Boston, anywhere, New York, any of those places. Couldn't stay in a white hotel. No, sir. The place we got our name, the Cotton Club, only one colored was allowed in there, and that was Bill Robinson.
Yeah, you told me about him.
Yeah, he was the only one. The only one they'd let in there. And he got in there through his Uncle Tomming and all that, I guess.
Like, in a lot of the travelling and

Well, whites, they would take that because they would be making money on it. Like cleaning clothes. But no eating, no, you couldn't eat in white restaurants. Colored restaurants, which were better, anyway.
If you were in an area where you couldn't find any -- say, if you were someplace in, say, somewhere in --
In the United States.
Say, you were someplace in Connecticut or someplace, where you were playing a job where there wasn't -- where there weren't any black restaurants, how would you get your food then?
[You had] colored restaurants.
Anywhere that you went, you always had one, so you never had a problem.

Yeah, we knew where they were. Yes, we knew. (Unintelligible) House where they served meals. We knew every place, never fooled around with white women or nothing like that. Prejudiced, didn't want them in the first place, even if you did want them you were on the leary side, because you never knew -- they were lynching back then, tarring and feathering.
Even in the North?
Yeah. They'd make it hard on you,

if they see you try to make a white woman. Not biting my tongue, they can't touch me now. I do what I want to do, I'm just that belligerent. Even though I'm married, it'll be 39 years this August 19, to the same woman. But who needs it? I don't need it. I don't need no woman. But my own Aline Eileen Crawford. That's the only thing I need, the only woman. The rest, I'm a good, jovial greeter. As Willie Smith used to say, here comes Craw (unintelligible), that's Jimmy Crawford, that great, big smile and he just turn everything around, when he walk in. Everybody, let's have a ball. I'm so glad I don't drink any whisky. Greatest step I took in my life, because eventually it will catch up with you.
Well, was there much -- speaking of the interracial romance -- no, before that, now, how did the -- like, you said, everyplace that bands went, they knew all of the --
They knew.
-- all of the places they would go and get food.

Oh, yeah, (unintelligible hundreds of) colored, black bands travelling up and down the roads. It was the only way they could work, because you couldn't work on no white restaurants and big shows and all those beautiful places like we had after we left Lakeside, Ohio and Lake Erie. Went to a job -- I told you about that.
So did the guys --
I didn't finish (inaudible).
Oh, excuse me.
When we finished Lakeside, Ohio, the summer of 1929, we had a job at Willie's Lake Shore Garden in Paineville, Ohio. When we got there, there was a rail strike and a musicians' strike.
Now, this was the height of Depression.
You told me about that.
Yes, we got that down, that's okay.

Now, what I was going to ask you about, so then, for instance, when the guys would be hanging out together, would they be giving each other information about the places you could eat or get your clothes cleaned?
That's right.
If you say, well, we got some gigs in Connecticut, --
Where can we eat, sleep and get our clothes cleaned. Yes, we talked that over.
Okay, then then would you --

Then they would know where to go when they hit the town? Well, where did you stay? Knew you couldn't stay in a white hotel. We'd tell them, go to Mother's in Boston, and Providence, go to such-and-such, and New Haven, go to such-and-such. I can't call them.
Oh, well, yeah, there's so many.
And eat here, good food. Yes, indeed, they really had good food.

How did people look at musicians then? I know you told me, one person told your wife that she shouldn't be messing around with a musician and a drummer at that, but that wasn't the way that people looked at musicians, was it?
No, what they thought of musicians was just an ordinary profession. That -- in other words, they weren't completely looked down on, unless they brought it about themselves.
Musicians in the Lunceford band were altogether different. They were looked up to, yeah, they were in a different category. That was a clean band.
Were there any other bands that were looked up to that you --

Duke Ellington. It all depended on on one musician and the personalities that different bands had. Other bands, oh, -- but Lunceford, Duke Ellington, and Cab Calloway got pretty popular there at one time, they were looked up to. There were something, struggling, other bands, they were looked down on.
What were the bands that were looked down on?

That I can't tell you. As a matter of fact, I just don't want to pinpoint them because I don't want to be in a libel suit or nothing like that. But there were many. I can name three that were looked up to.
Now, you know when they send you the transcription back, you can bracket that as something that you don't want published.
Well, I remember some experiences that I was told, like, for instance, catch a guy like -- what was this bass player with Duke Ellington's band? Not Pettiford,
Wellman Braud?
Huh?
Wellman Braud?
No, not him. He was nice. He can't call his name. Aline knows. Aline? [I think she] told me this one, about -- is it on?
Yeah, it's on.
About (inaudible), can't call --
Billy Taylor?
No, not him. Aline Eileen.
Let me see, he had a bass player named Raglin Ragman.
Raglin Ragman, Junior Raglin Ragman.
Junior Ragman, yeah.
I think that's the one. In the bus,
on the train, bands that could afford to ride trains, like Raglin Ellington, -- Junior Ragman, he played with Ellington.
Yeah.

Well, he had a habit -- he was a kleptomaniac, and he had a habit, when everybody would sleep, he would go by and find a bottle of booze, take him a good swig or two out of it. That's the way he'd get his kicks. He would get his kicks. And so, he went by one time, and a tenor saxophone player in Ellington's band, looked like white (unintelligible) saw his picture from New Orleans -- it was on your book, (unintelligible) right there on the cover.
You mean Barney Begard?

Barney Begard. You know what happened? Stan, sit down a minute, boy, this is funny. Old Junior would go by, and he was a natural kleptomaniac, and stealing booze from everybody. Well, he found a bottle behind the seat or beside the seat. He would grab it and take him a good swig.

And so Barney Begard one time tricked him, and he peed in the bottle. And Old Junior, thinking it was booze, it was all the same color, man, he upped that bottle and swallowed that stuff. And so Barney says, now, I hope you know what you just did. Boy, those guys used to do a lot of things. (Unintelligible) told me about that.
You told me about the alarm clocks.
Oh, yeah, Jack Carruthers.
Yeah, you told me about that.
Yeah, and Paul Webster.
Was there much practical --
Yeah, he was a practical joker.
Were many musicians practical jokers in those days?

No, but these guys were just free to do anything because they had been working with Lunceford's band for so long, and that alarm clock would go off at the most atrocious hour after a gig. The guys would be sleeping. Jack Carruthers did it. He was a real practical joker.
Were the guys in those periods -- did they read much? I don't mean music, but did many of the guys --
Willie Smith.
He read a lot of books and stuff?

Always, always reading. He was a peculiar person. He was from Charleston, South Carolina, so he'd be sitting there, reading, smoking a cigarette, always had a book in front of him, always, when he was walking the streets, always was reading. He had a bottle of whisky. And so -- didn't read much. I taught myself how to read more like periodicals, newspapers, books and et cetera, recently. And -- but Willie Smith always had a book. And so,

you'd go by and you'd say, hey, Willie, excuse me a minute. Now, you're interrupting him from reading. Will you give me a cigarette, please? You weren't doing to be -- for no joke. I wanted a cigarette.

So Willie while reading just slip in his pockets and hand me -- no, first he would take out a cigarette, take the cigarette out and take the pack and lay it over, like that. And Willie would say a prayer to himself, first, before he gave me that cigarette. And he'd hand you the cigarette. And I was wondering what that was all about, and never did know, even today, even though Willie's dead. I didn't know what that prayer business -- well, he's a Greek, that's all.
So that was his way of doing things. He'd always lay that cigarette on that pack and then say a prayer. Then he'd take that cigarette and then give it to me. I didn't know.
Yeah, he is very unusual.
Very unusual.
Were many musicians very aware of politics and stuff in those days? Did they talk much about presidents prejudice?
No.
No political interest.
No, because most of the people in
the South, the colored people, they were Republicans. No Democrats around (Inaudible). I just found that out (inaudible).
Did many musicians vote, register to vote and stuff?
No, not our men. Of course, now I vote in every election.
What about Smith? Did Willie Smith vote? Or Lunceford?

Not that I know of, no. Up until Roosevelt, I think that opened their eyes quite a bit, opened their eyes quite a bit, because that man did quite a bit. People like President Abraham Lincoln, who was an abolitionist, that's why they killed him, get him out of the way.
Well, some people say that's why they think they killed Huey Long, too, because he was doing some of these programs --
Oh, in Louisiana.
Yeah, some of these programs were helping --
Helping blacks.
Yeah, that's what some people think.
Well, he was a pretty liberal-minded man. Even though he was a staunch Southerner. People like FDR and that President Truman, beautiful man. He'd stand on

his rights, and he was a liberal-minded President, him. Roosevelt and Truman and Carter, the present President. Now, I'm hoping and praying to God nothing will ever happen to him, because these damn bigots, you never know. He'll come out in the open and tell you, he's a Baptist, also. Black and whites, what's the difference?
Oh, I know what I was going to ask you. There was a period in the late '30s, Rex Stewart was talking about it, late '30s and '40s, when there was --
You mention Rex quite a bit. You must know him --
Well, he wrote a lot, you know. Rex wrote a lot of essays about the '30s. In fact, --
I didn't know that.
In fact, I'll tell you what. Next time I see this book he wrote, called Jazz Masters of the 1930's, I'll get you a copy.
Thank you. Tell him Jimmy Crawford wants it. And he knows I will try my utmost to read it.
Well, he was saying that there was a period where people were writing a lot of tunes and had a African titles and references to it, like (he did one called "Menelik") (singing). Anyway, --
You were playing bop, then. (Unintelligible.) (cresc).
Did you ever play those kind of pieces,
used mallets like pieces, ballads on the tom-toms and stuff like -- he said it was based in the late '30s. Do you remember any of that?
I'm pretty sure I did, but I don't remember what-all I did. Which was very little, at that. But I got a effect of it, and I liked it. Used to play those rhythms, (Sambas,) Latin types.
When did you start playing Latin type rhythms in the '30s? Is that when they started having a --
Yeah, revolutionizing, putting it all in there.
Well, there was a period when --
Sambas and mambas and all that kind of stuff.
Those were popular in the '30s?
No, not to us. Not to us. Not Jimmy Lunceford. He didn't play much of that.
