Did many bands play much of that? Because, I saw a movie with --
Well, you had bands. You had Machito and renaissance and all those things. That was on the bandstand at one time?
Mario Bauza (Unintelligible), do you remember his band?
No, I didn't. Mario --
Mario Bauza.
Yeah, I heard him, he was a good trumpet player. Wasn't he a trumpet player?
Yeah, Dizzy used to go and sit in.
Yeah, Mario was a good, legitimate trumpet player. Oh, yes.
Well, let's go -- like, again, when you were in the service, when you started playing in the service, did you start reading (out of drumbooks then) (inaudible) or --
Oh, yes. That's when that other drummer by the name of Buster, he was a West Indian boy, big, strong rascal, he bet those -- that practice pad, down at the bottom of those little --
The supports to hold the legs?
Yeah, he used to put those big old Army shoes on there and bend that practice pad. He'd get me pretty steamed up, because that same pad right there --
You've had this same pad since you went in the Army in 1942?
Oh, yes, I went in there with it.
And you started using this pad to study out of the books.
Yeah.
That's when you started learning how to play the Army marches and stuff like that?
Yeah, I had to practice those. And
read. [—] still, (inaudible).

Did you have to play any of those pieces -- like, I was listening to something by Louis Armstrong, -- you said yesterday, where you go from a march to kind of what -- well, Jelly Roll Morton called it a Spanish tinge, where they'd start off (singing), there'd be a march --
And then they'd go into swing.
Yeah, they'd go into that.
In the Army we did that. Not too much in Lunceford's band. We started out like it was supposed to be, and --
When you got out of the service -- you didn't see any action, as far as bang-bang, boom-boom.

When I got out of the service, I happened to run into Mary Lou Williams, who I knew very well in Memphis. And she told me to go by and see Ed Hall at Cafe Society uptown. And that's when I started peeping through the (unintelligible) cracks on the outside every night, to see what drummer was doing. Trap Hull from Brooklyn, playing good.
cracks
Trap Hull
peeping through the
And I used to go by every night.
What was the difference that you noticed, in terms of the difference in the way that he was playing?
Well, he was playing the way it was supposed to be. He was playing a show, and Mary Lou Williams,

Hazel Scott, people like that appearing there. And he was playing good. So I had to see because I hadn't played -- I'm coming out of a big band. Now, Ed Hall had a small band, so I had to learn how to do it.
But did you -- what is the difference that you see between playing for a small band and playing for a big band?

Altogether a great difference. A great difference. You're exposed on every number, everything you play. Drums are only about six or seven pieces. Big band, you got a whole lot of help. But there's a big difference.
So do you think that the small -- a guy playing in a small band has to have his technical things in better shape? Is that what you're saying?
Yeah, he was exposed more.
Because he's not --

It's rough, but this small band drummer really got to hold up his drums. In other words, play your drums to fit in accordingly with the other musicians -- trombone, trumpet, piano and bass, clarinet, maybe five to seven pieces, mostly five -- piano, drummer, bass player, trumpet, trombone and clarinet, from five to seven pieces.
Did you use the set differently? Did you play the cymbals more or less, or you used to play more the snare drum, more or less?
No, you've got to fit yourself in and play your cymbals, but play them accordingly, taste and touch. I was no technical drummer then.
Oh, I see what you're saying, because when you don't have that volume of the big band, then that's --
Help, I call it. Yes, and so, it's a difference.
To keep from overbearing the --
Yes. Well, do you think we --

Let's see, we've got the end of this one and we've got about a half hour more. I can talk with you about your experiences in your shows and stuff, and we'll just about have finished it up. I think we will have finished it. We're almost at the end of this one.
So you were saying that you've got to have more control -- you're saying in a certain sense, you have to have more control in a smaller --
Yeah.
You have to have more dynamic.
Yes. No, not dynamic-wise, just fit in. It's a close knitted thing there, because every instrument stands out within itself, every instrument.
Did you take [many] solos when you were working in Hall's band?
In Ed Hall's -- no, I didn't know how
to. I'd take breaks, but seles --
(End of Side Two.)
-- Jimmy Crawford, last section. All right, now, when you got out of the service, you worked with Ed Hall's band.
Uh-huh.
And how long did you work in that band?
Oh, about five years, both uptown in cafe society and downtown in Cafe Society.
Had -- around that time, when you got out of the service, -- what year did you get out of the service, do you remember?
1945. Well, the bebop movement was in sway, then, too, wasn't it?
After that, I think.
What did you think of them when you heard that happening?
That era, of bebop?
Uh-huh.
I didn't care too much for it. I was used to swinging.
You didn't think that the bebop drummers were swinging?
No, I didn't think so. And -- well,

if I had the execution that Art Blakey's got, I don't know where he came from. He just came up, and he can play. Beautiful drummer, accents and whatnot. I don't know where he came from, but that rascal sure can play. Max Roach and all that batch, Max [got something from them too]. (Inaudible) Oh, yeah.
Clarke
What about Kenny Clarke?
He got some from Blakey, and he was within his own right, he was a good drummer. My dear friend, Kenny Clarke.
How do you think about him as a swinger? Do you think he could swing?
Yeah, he could swing. He could play most anything. Wide brushes, sticks, swing, bop, he was good. I wonder what happened to him?
He's in Paris.
Oh, yeah?
He's in Paris. I saw him not too long ago. He was in New York for a little while.
Yeah, he was a good all-around drummer.
Yeah, he still sounds beautiful. So did you have occasion to play with any of the bebop musicians, like Dizzy Gillespie or Charlie Parker?
No. No, I think I played with Dizzy, but not the rest of them -- Charlie Parker and Bud Powell and all them, no.
You knew Dizzy Gillespie fairly well, didn't you?
Very well.
Where did you meet him?
Philadelphia.
You met him in Philadelphia?
Yeah.
Was he still in Cab Calloway's band when you met him?
No, he was just gigging by himself. He's responsible for bringing in bebop. He and Charlie Parker. But Dizzy was the man, he's a great trumpet player.
Did you think he swung in bebop style?
I didn't want to hear that. Again. What did you say?
Did you think that within the bebop style, that Dizzy was swinging?
Yeah, in his type of way, he could swing. He was an all-around trumpet player.
What was it about bebop that you -- bothered you in terms of the swinging?
The drummers and the players. I didn't like it at first, and happened to be -- I happened to listen a little bit more, don't like it right now. I'm as I forestated a swinger, (inaudible).
Do you think it's because they didn't play four quarter notes on the bass drum?
Yeah. Drummers got out of hand. They just didn't play the way I like a drummer to play. In other words, like sounds they were getting, I just didn't like it. Couldn't swing, shame on you.

That's right, and so I didn't go for it, at all. I thought it was a bunch of noise, especially the drummers. Kenny Clarke is an all-around drummer. Max Roach (Unintelligible) is another all-around drummer. Rest of 'em...
What about Roy Haynes? He was a --
Roy Haynes was a combo drummer. I don't care if he played in the big bands, the swing wasn't there. Wasn'ta blues drummer. Good drummer, though.
You felt good about the way Blakey played.
Oh, Blakey good (inaudible) all-around drummer.
Now, when you -- so after you had worked with Hall's band for a few years, that's when you began to work --
Small combos.
Yeah, you worked other small bands besides his?
Yeah, Ben Webster.
How was that? How was the experience of working in his band?

Oh, Ben was rough on you. He couldn't stand piano players like Billy Taylor, his style of playing. He wanted that old piano style-- not only style, but he just wanted a swinging piano player, and he used to have them quite often, [he and] Billy Taylor.

Ben didn't like that man. Didn't like his playing, he liked him maybe as a person, but he couldn't stand his playing. Ben was from the school of -- the swinging school. So I'd go along with him. I was, too.
Who else was in the band with you when you were with Webster?
I don't remember.
Did you work with him long?
Yeah, I worked in some club. I can't recall what club.
Was he as rough and violent and wild as people say he was?

Not on the bandstand. He just didn't like Billy Taylor's piano playing. Other than that, we got along swell, that's all that mattered to me. If we didn't get along, hell, I'd walk off the bandstand, I'd quit. I didn't care. As hungry as I was. (Inaudible) regard him or nobody, I don't care who it was. And I was nobody. I just
got to be staunch in my way. I don't have to be, but I am. I'm stubborn, too.
Who were some of the more exciting people that you played with in that period, before you started working shows? With Ed Hall, and you worked with Ben Webster.
I worked with a lot of combos.
Benny Goodman.
Benny Goodman, Sidney Bechet.
How was that? What was --
Oh, now, that was a tough man, Sidney Bechet. Man, that man was tough. I didn't stay with him long. Of course, I just went on a job with him. He was tough.
When you say tough, what do you mean?

Tough to work with. He's -- he was noted to be tough. Was just a tough old New Orleans player. You He know the style he plays, just stomping. He was the only one that deserved any credit for it. I just didn't like working for him.
What did he want you to play, like, a lot of press rolls and --

Oh, just play swing. He never did bother me. He never bothered me, for some reason. Well, I didn't give a darn, because he'd get it right back from me. Or either I'd pack up my drum and tell my wife, come pick me
up. Pick me up, because I'm coming home. I quit this band. I was a big band drummer, and I still am. But now I can adjust myself to any band.

And so, I was talking about my tenants downstairs. I hear them hollering down there, and I'm going to try to get rid of them. I've been telling that them quite a number of times. And so I want to get rid of them, and I want to get them out of my house, because I demand respect, I don't ask for it.

Now, when you were -- so around the time you were working these bands, you began to go into -- oh, there was one thing I forgot to ask you. Was there much of a difference in the scene, the musical scene in New York, when you got out of the Army as opposed to when you went in? Had things begun to change any?

Yeah. Guys stopped swinging. When I finally noticed came out, I find (inaudible). So I asked somebody, man, why do you all play like that? We was talking about someplace I was playing. Why do you all play with that old bebop? Why better for me to play the way I'm don't you play modern? Say, well, (inaudible) way-out playing. Why do you play the way you play? Making a lot of unnecessary noise and stuff.
So that's all. I finally realized that I learned all over again my approach to music.
But, now, you have over here, you have
Many of them.
-- which is -- Chapin's book, which is mostly --
Chapin.
Chapin, excuse me.
Exercises.
But it's mostly like about -- this is like a bebop style. A lot of these things are bebop style things that -- you've gone through this book, too, though.
Oh, yeah. Thing of it is, in there they're mostly exercises, with your foot and your hands. They have two lines there for drumming, modern drumming, they call it. And so --
What did you think about these things after you went through the book?
A great deal about them. Helped me out in my technique and playing, and independence, mostly.
Were drummers playing with much independence before the bebop style?
No.
So that --
Straight down the middle. Bebop brought in a lot of independence. Just like a piano player.
So, now, you were saying that you felt
like a lot of independence came in with the bebop. Did you want to eat your sandwich before we finish?
I'm going to eat it -- I'll eat it afterwards.
Okay. I mean, if you wanted to, I can wait.
No, I want to get it over with.
Okay.
(Recording interrupted.)
So, now, at the end of the '40s, after playing with a variety of small groups, you began to become interested in working in shows?
Yeah.
How did this take place?

Well, (unintelligible), Billy Kyle was a rehearsal pianist and a for a of Broadway show. And so they wanted a swinging colored drummer. So Billy went home to his wife, and they talked it over, and she said, well, what about Craw? He says, oh, yes, Craw, that's an ideal person. He's a gentleman and he can read and so he said, yeah, call him.

So Billy Kyle called me, and asked me did I want to do a show, a Broadway musical. I had never played a Broadway musical, and so from then on, that's when they started calling me. I would make a scale, a union scale, first and as I grew

bigger in the business and got all those calls, one after another, I began asking for money. And they started paying me good money, good money. All of them, Ethel Merman, Carol Channing, Carol Bruce, Gwen Verdon, different shows. I can't call the names of the shows, but I played over 20 Broadway musicals. Over.
Well, you mentioned earlier that it was around this time that you began to study the drums very --
Yeah.
Did you study them after you worked your first show or before?
No. This was after.
After you began working the shows.

Yeah, shows. I knew that I had to have something else. I started to studying xylophones to try to become a percussionist, and I got the xylophones up there now. And so I just had to study, for all the pride and everything else behind me.
So I did. Every Saturday I'd take me a lesson. Drumming. I studied mostly on the practice pad. And it helped out a great deal.
So what were you studying? Were you studying just, like, rudiments or reed --
Rudiments.
Just studying rudiments.

Rudiments. No independence, just rudiments. And I'm glad I did. Like, rudiments is, like, paradiddles (unintelligible), flamadiddles and such things as that. And different strokes, different rolls, five-stroke roll, seven-stroke roll, threes, whatnot. And so it helped me out tremendously.
And so I'm glad I did it. And right today, I'm still studying rudiments, yes, sir.
And so you were using, like, -- had you been using -- you had been in your years before been playing many rudiments, or --
No. None. Just getting up there and beating on some drums. That's all I was doing.
But you must have been using --
Well, self, myself, kind of listened and played what the bands -- whoever you're playing with, you got to play.
So, now, when the shows that -- how did you -
They were a challenge.
What made them challenging?

You had to read and you had to think, even though you were sitting in the pit, with about a 30 or some piece band, 35, 40, I don't remember. Full set of band -- strings, harps, bassoons, oboes, all the instruments that
consist of a pit orchestra. Very few that I went onstage with.
You were the only black musician in the band.
Yeah.
Did you find --

Most of the shows, I was the only black. Eventually they started getting other guys in there, like, when Sammy Davis would come in and do a Broadway musical, like Apple Tree, Golden Boy, Mr. Wonderful, I played all of them. I played them like I was playing in a band. That's what they liked about me, authoritative drumming, not down there trying to show off or nothing. Sit back and play your music. So I enjoyed that period of time, really enjoyed it, although it was tiresome and monotonous. You go in and you do your first show and so I did the best I could.
Now, did you find much difference in kinds of musicians that worked in the pit orchestras in the shows and the musicians that worked in the many bands that you've worked in?
A great difference. Those guys were longhair players. Me, I'm a swinger. So that's what they wanted me then to do, to boot that band, even though they were longhair men.
See, a choreographer such as Jack Cole, people like that, they wanted a drummer in there to play that show and

try to make those (cold) longhair guys swing. Well, I did the best I could. And they kept calling me and so I kept demanding more and more money. And they would give it to me. I couldn't play for cheap. Right today, I'm the same way.
So, if they're going to loan these tapes out again, I'd say, send me my residuals, and subsidies and et cetera.
Now, you also began to do a lot of studio work, too, in that period, didn't you?
Quite a lot. Very much. Making records for all the big names that's even today -- Sammy Davis, just keep naming, Perry Como, kept me on his show.
Oh, you worked his television show, too, didn't you?
Oh, yeah, I worked (inaudible).
Were there many black musicians working on the television shows?

No, there were only two black musicians, and they were both drummers, on Broadway, playing big television shows and recordings. There were two, Specs Powell and Jimmy Crawford, two drummers. Yeah, Specs was a very good professional drummer, all around drummer. He played -- he was a percussionist. And so, me, I wasn't and that was one of the reasons I started studying, to try to get like him.
But there were only two, two black drummers on
Broadway.
Why do you think there was only two black musicians?
They knew they couldn't trust them, nor would they fit in that surrounding. But they knew that -- I'm sorry.
Because of the reading?

Well, whatever it was. I don't know offhand, but I know they knew that we would cut it, in what we did. Only two, Specs Powell, he lives in Jamaica now, somewhere, and I'm still here in New York and I'm still going, although I have retired.
How did you feel about working the television shows?
No difference. I was at home.
Your wife mentioned earlier that there was a favorite tune of Perry Como's that he always wanted to have you play.

Yeah, the name of the tune was Kokomo. And that I played. I just had a knack of it. I knew how to play it. It wasn't hard, just played time, it wasn't hard, peculiar about it. Perry was a beautiful person, can't meet a better one. I've recorded Perry Como, Sammy Davis and don't mention the work that I did for Mitch Miller.
Oh, you worked for Mitch Miller.
Leslie Uggams
{Unintelligible} and all of them. I can tell you some things, but I won't put that on the tape. So --
Well, now, as I said, you can --

No, I won't, uh-huh, not what I'm thinking, which is all right. Yeah, I worked a lot for Mitch Miller. Just name them all, they all were engineers, like, and directors for the date. Jackie Gleason, everything he made, I was on it. All his records. Fortunately, I have them Silk and Shookin' Brass and all of them.
So you and Bobby Hackett -- well, you were on the sessions and Bobby Hackett.
Yeah, yeah, I was right there.
How did you and Hackett feel about the other musicians that you worked with? You are were about the only jazz musicians on those --

That's right. We felt that we were there to support the longhairs that were on the date. Capital, Victor, Columbia, just many, many, most every day. I find myself in a studio after the shows, after the run, or before the shows. It went overtime, I had to leave, but they would cut it short and make it come out on time for my benefit. They knew I wasn't going to be late for my Broadway musical. And I had to finish the job. Max Mae Sepos was a big contractor, various other big contractors.
Were you as happy working in those situations as you had been when you were working in jazz bands?

I was as happy, because I had thrown the jazz band out of my mind. And I was trying to do my job for the person -- for whom the person's job. Recordings and musicals, that was my stick. I enjoyed doing it.

Well, because I know Quincy Jones spoke highly of you, and I was wondering, did you feel a relief from, say, the monotony of working in the shows, when you got a chance to do a date where you got to play with musicians that didn't play the same thing all the time?

Well, about that, Quincy Jones was nice enough to call me. Also, he called Milt Hinton on bass, the date was Dinah Washington record date. And so Quincy was very, very pleased with the work we did, because he said the drumming situation today is completely out of hand. He wants some guys that play, just play. And Dinah did Lady D or something, I can't recall. I have the records here somewhere.

But, as I said, I want to get this over, because I'm going up and -- I'm going to finish my sandwich, then I'm going up and take me a little nap. If I wake up fresh, I be thinking about you, Stanley. And say, now let's start all over again. But I'm going to try to finish this off, and look forward to my -- if I have any shortcomings on these
put a bracket around them
tapes, just (inaudible) or indicate on them, do the best you can, because I'm tired physically and mentally, mostly mentally.
Yeah, I was born in 1910, and it's taken -- I've paid a lot of dues. And for my memos and experiences, both here and abroad.
Oh, the last closeout. Did you -- when did you officially retire from playing?

Oh, my wife knows the date, knows the year. Anything, she knows the date. So she'll be down in a minute. I don't want to holler loud over the tape. But Aline, I'm going to just whisper. Eileen. Well, she went upstairs.

Well, I can ask you another thing then. When did you begin to notice -- well, you mentioned something off the tape, I think, the last time I was talking to you, about there were musicians who were telling you that they weren't interested in playing shows.

Oh, yeah. Yeah, there were musicians and they'd get down for the lack of an income, they thought a Broadway show was a letdown to them. So let them think it, and they thought it. But they're back there now, looking for Broadway musicals and anything else they can think of to play. To me, I enjoyed it, and I did the very best I could.
Okay, last --
I'm writing a book, you know.
Oh, you're writing a book?

Yeah, and I've just about completed it. I started it a year ago, or a little over. And so, that will be the title of it, if I can get on with the purpose of it. The title will be, I did the very best I could. That's the title. That's what I hope the publisher will go for.
Presently I have three or four publishers that want to publish the book, especially Stanley Dance. He's my dear friend. He's done a lot to help me out in everything. And so he's a dear, dear friend.
Yeah, that's his wife, Helen Oakley. Came over here from Great Britain. Stanley did, and I just love that man, I really do.
Well, I think to close out, I would like to ask you about the yacht caps and Atlantic City.

Well, I don't know, I had me an urge to wear a captain's cap, whether it was white or whether it was Navy blue, or dark. I just loved to wear them while in Atlantic City, because we went there for every summer for quite a number of years, my wife and I. And all of a sudden, I looked up, Count Basie had one on. Lena Horne's husband, Lennie Hayton had and he hated to have one on all the time. Well, they must have saw me with it and they liked it and thought it appropriate.
So that's all I got to say about that. So I wore my hat all the time.
Okay, Mr. Crawford. Well, thank you very much for the interview. I think we've got five hours of material here, I'm not sure.

I hope so. If not, we can set it up again. But I don't want to overdo it, but I always give a little spare, and I hope we have enough. So thank you, and thank you, Smithsonian Institute, for including in your plans for a great, great tribute that is paid me. I really appreciate it. And thanks again for a great tribute.
(End of proceedings as recorded.)

segments.chapter: Memphis boyhood and the Ohio territory years
segments.title: Opening of the interview at Crawford's Bronx home
segments.summary: Crouch opens the Smithsonian interview, giving the date and place, and Crawford jokes about starting at the beginning.

segments.chapter: Memphis boyhood and the Ohio territory years
segments.title: Orphaned in Memphis and raised by illiterate grandparents
segments.summary: Crawford recalls starting in high school in Memphis, losing his parents young and being raised by his grandparents, his grandmother a famed midwife.

segments.chapter: Memphis boyhood and the Ohio territory years
segments.title: Jimmy Lunceford, the athletic instructor who formed the band
segments.summary: Crawford describes Lunceford's Fisk and Columbia background, his return to Memphis, and the band's summers at Lakeside and move north to Cleveland.

segments.chapter: Memphis boyhood and the Ohio territory years
segments.title: Starving in Cleveland during the musicians' and waiters' strike
segments.summary: The band hits Cleveland in a strike, goes hungry, and Crawford contrasts Lunceford's lack of arrangements with Ralph Cooper's meal deals for his show.

segments.chapter: Memphis boyhood and the Ohio territory years
segments.title: Route from Cleveland to Buffalo to the New York Cotton Club
segments.summary: Crouch pins down dates as the band travels by Ford from Cleveland and Cincinnati to Buffalo and then to New York and the Cotton Club.

segments.chapter: Memphis boyhood and the Ohio territory years
segments.title: The booker who ran off with the money
segments.summary: Crawford tells how a Cleveland booker fled with the band's pay and Lunceford, Eddie Wilcox and he chased him down in a Ford.

segments.chapter: Memphis boyhood and the Ohio territory years
segments.title: Nineteen dollars with pianist Bobbie Brown and a bag of hot dogs
segments.summary: Crawford takes a two-person gig with pianist Bobbie Brown in Cleveland and spends the pay on hot dogs for the hungry band.

segments.chapter: Memphis boyhood and the Ohio territory years
segments.title: Booker Washington, the Memphis pit drummer who inspired him
segments.summary: Crawford explains that Booker Washington at the Palace Theater on Beale Street, with his stick tricks, made him want to be a drummer.

segments.chapter: Career overview and the Lunceford quarrel
segments.title: Buying a full Leedy drum set for the Cotton Club
segments.summary: Crawford explains the quarrel with Lunceford: told to have drums for the Cotton Club, he paid about $1,600 for a set on $60 a week while Lunceford bought no uniforms.

segments.chapter: Career overview and the Lunceford quarrel
segments.title: Bill Robinson tells Lunceford to pay him off
segments.summary: In a theater, Bill Robinson's valet gives Lunceford money to pay off Crawford with a racial slur, and Crawford still resents Robinson.

segments.chapter: Career overview and the Lunceford quarrel
segments.title: Fourteen years with Lunceford, then the Army at Camp Kilmer
segments.summary: Crawford says he drummed with Lunceford for 14 years until drafted, then played in an Army Service Force band at Camp Kilmer.

segments.chapter: Career overview and the Lunceford quarrel
segments.title: Mary Lou Williams sends him to Cafe Society and Ed Hall
segments.summary: After the Army, Mary Lou Williams steers him past the 802 union problem to a job with Ed Hall's group at Cafe Society, where he had peeked at the drummer.

segments.chapter: Career overview and the Lunceford quarrel
segments.title: Broadway musicals, records and buying the Bronx house
segments.summary: Crawford describes playing over 21 Broadway musicals starting with a Billy Kyle show, making records, and paying off his large house in two years.

segments.chapter: Learning the drums and early influences
segments.title: Crouch redirects to childhood; Booker Washington, Chick Webb and Buddy Rich
segments.summary: Crouch asks to fill in the childhood details, and Crawford repeats that Booker Washington was the most sensational drummer he saw, alongside Chick Webb and Buddy Rich.

segments.chapter: Learning the drums and early influences
segments.title: Early jobs to save for drums and starting on the peck horn
segments.summary: Crawford says his school had no drum set, so he picked cotton and did odd jobs; he started on the peck horn.

segments.chapter: Learning the drums and early influences
segments.title: Teaching himself drums and learning paradiddles from Cozy Cole
segments.summary: He had no teacher, learned on the job in Lunceford's band, and later asked Cozy Cole how to play ratamacues and paradiddles.

segments.chapter: Learning the drums and early influences
segments.title: Stealing from other drummers and the first beats he played
segments.summary: Crawford says he learned by watching, played four on the bass drum with press rolls, and loves his drums.

segments.chapter: Learning the drums and early influences
segments.title: Zutty Singleton, Baby Dodds and New Orleans drummers he never heard
segments.summary: Crawford knew Zutty in New York, only knew of Baby Dodds, and did not hear King Oliver's or Armstrong's bands as a boy.

segments.chapter: Learning the drums and early influences
segments.title: Alphonso Trent's band, A. G. Gardner and Stuff Smith
segments.summary: Crawford calls Alphonso Trent's Little Rock band the most impressive he heard, praising drummer A. G. Gardner's northern style.

segments.chapter: Learning the drums and early influences
segments.title: Booker Washington's stick twirling, horns and pistols
segments.summary: Crawford describes how Booker Washington twirled and threw sticks and used squeeze horns and blank pistols while playing.

segments.chapter: Learning the drums and early influences
segments.title: Sock cymbals and Kaiser Marshall's high hat
segments.summary: Crawford describes the flat floor sock cymbal and says Kaiser Marshall was the first he saw play a high hat.

segments.chapter: Learning the drums and early influences
segments.title: Northern and southern drumming styles and Joe Jones with Basie
segments.summary: Crawford contrasts the southern snare-and-choke style with the freer northern style and praises Joe Jones, subbing for him at the Club Harlem.

segments.chapter: Learning the drums and early influences
segments.title: High school playing with no practice, and the first big bass drum
segments.summary: He did not practice, played stock arrangements, and describes his first huge bass drum, later made into a coffee table.

segments.chapter: Learning the drums and early influences
segments.title: The first drum set and playing the back beat
segments.summary: Crawford and Crouch reconstruct his first set of bass drum, snare and small sock cymbal, played on two and four.

segments.chapter: Learning the drums and early influences
segments.title: Arguing with Sy Oliver over two beats and four beats
segments.summary: Crawford recalls arguments with Sy Oliver about riding out the last chorus in four versus two, and how Sy still hired him on every date.

segments.chapter: Learning the drums and early influences
segments.title: Playing breaks on 'I'm Nuts About Screwy Music'
segments.summary: Crouch asks about the breaks on Lunceford recordings; Crawford says they were written in as four-bar or two-bar breaks and he just played them.

segments.chapter: Learning the drums and early influences
segments.title: Hearing Chick Webb, Kaiser Marshall and Zutty after reaching New York
segments.summary: Crawford says he heard Chick Webb nightly in New York and describes Zutty's New Orleans style.

segments.chapter: Buffalo years and Lunceford's discipline
segments.title: Buffalo college jobs and segregated hotels
segments.summary: The band worked colleges and clubs around Buffalo and stayed in colored hotels such as the Vendome and the Sterling in Cincinnati.

segments.chapter: Buffalo years and Lunceford's discipline
segments.title: Hustlers and number men at the Vendome Hotel
segments.summary: Crawford describes the numbers bankers who stayed at the hotels and the Core and Claw families of Buffalo, with a detour on food at the Howard.

segments.chapter: Buffalo years and Lunceford's discipline
segments.title: Stock arrangements until Sy Oliver and Willie Smith
segments.summary: Crawford says the band played stocks until Sy Oliver arrived and contributed greatly, with Willie Smith and Wilcox also writing.

segments.chapter: Buffalo years and Lunceford's discipline
segments.title: Lunceford's strict manners and the band's class
segments.summary: Crawford explains that Lunceford acted like a father who demanded respect, dress and rehearsal, and neither drank, smoked nor cursed.

segments.chapter: Buffalo years and Lunceford's discipline
segments.title: Crawford and Al Norris as the band's drinkers
segments.summary: Crawford says he was the ringleader who drank with Al Norris and Willie Smith, while Wilcox drank little.

segments.chapter: Buffalo years and Lunceford's discipline
segments.title: Late only once, with Elliott Lawrence's show, and Freddie Webster
segments.summary: Crawford says he was late once in 45 years, during a Broadway show, and recalls Freddie Webster could not keep time.

segments.chapter: Buffalo years and Lunceford's discipline
segments.title: Lunceford's manners and his brother Connie
segments.summary: Crouch probes Lunceford's discipline and Crawford talks about his family and his valet brother Connie, a heavy drinker.

segments.chapter: Buffalo years and Lunceford's discipline
segments.title: Crawford's recent hospital stay and diet
segments.summary: Crawford describes his checkups, a recent hospital stay after dropping to 129 pounds, and his diet.

segments.chapter: New York, the Lafayette and the Cotton Club
segments.title: Moving to New York and two weeks at the Lafayette Theater
segments.summary: Crawford gives his Harlem addresses and says the Lunceford band played the Lafayette for two weeks because it drew crowds, before the Cotton Club.

segments.chapter: New York, the Lafayette and the Cotton Club
segments.title: First recordings, Irving Mills and Will Hudson's arrangements
segments.summary: Crawford says the band first recorded in New York, was tied to Irving Mills's office, and he disliked Will Hudson's charts.

segments.chapter: New York, the Lafayette and the Cotton Club
segments.title: Lafayette vaudeville shows and meeting his wife in the chorus line
segments.summary: Crawford recalls playing for acts and a chorus line at the Lafayette and meeting his wife, a chorus girl, on the road with the band.

segments.chapter: New York, the Lafayette and the Cotton Club
segments.title: The Berry Brothers as the greatest act he saw
segments.summary: Crawford calls the Berry Brothers the greatest act he ever saw and describes their flips and struts.

segments.chapter: New York, the Lafayette and the Cotton Club
segments.title: Paying 60 cents to hear Fletcher Henderson in Cleveland
segments.summary: Arriving in Cleveland with $1.60, Crawford spends 60 cents to hear Fletcher Henderson's band with Coleman Hawkins.

segments.chapter: New York, the Lafayette and the Cotton Club
segments.title: Fletcher Henderson's difficult keys and brother Horace
segments.summary: Crawford says Henderson wrote in unusual keys that challenged players such as Roy Eldridge, and mentions Horace Henderson in Colorado.

segments.chapter: New York, the Lafayette and the Cotton Club
segments.title: Henderson's band, Hawkins and meeting Kaiser Marshall
segments.summary: Crawford recalls King Porter Stomp and Hawkins's featured playing, and going up to meet drummer Kaiser Marshall.

segments.chapter: New York, the Lafayette and the Cotton Club
segments.title: Territory bands he heard and the Moten-Basie link
segments.summary: Crawford says he never met Bennie Moten, notes Basie took over Moten's band, and lists Alphonso Trent, Speed Webb and Zack White as the best bands he heard.

segments.chapter: New York, the Lafayette and the Cotton Club
segments.title: Playing proms and schools for white audiences around Buffalo
segments.summary: Crawford says the band played proms and colleges, stayed in private colored homes, and played the same book everywhere.

segments.chapter: New York, the Lafayette and the Cotton Club
segments.title: Manhattan Center ball with Dorsey and Goodman's bands
segments.summary: Crawford recalls Lunceford's band being unable to leave the stand at a ball packed with the top bands.

segments.chapter: New York, the Lafayette and the Cotton Club
segments.title: The 802 union keeps Lunceford's band out; Peekaboo Davis
segments.summary: Crawford says Local 802 refused them membership to slow the band, a delegate named Peekaboo Davis policed it, and they used Buffalo's local 533.

segments.chapter: New York, the Lafayette and the Cotton Club
segments.title: Opening at the Cotton Club as house band for six months
segments.summary: Crawford describes the Cotton Club as the top New York club, the band's second job, replacing Cab Calloway as house band for about six months.

segments.chapter: New York, the Lafayette and the Cotton Club
segments.title: Bill Robinson as a tap dancer and the double standard
segments.summary: Crawford calls Bill Robinson the greatest tap dancer, better than Astaire, and comments that Black performers only recently gained wider opportunity.

segments.chapter: New York, the Lafayette and the Cotton Club
segments.title: Racial segregation answered with respect and upbringing
segments.summary: Asked how musicians reacted to segregation, Crawford says they demanded respect, as his grandparents, teachers and Lunceford taught him.

segments.chapter: New York, the Lafayette and the Cotton Club
segments.title: Competition among bands and Cab Calloway at the rehearsal
segments.summary: Crawford says rival bands did not want them, and Cab Calloway, also managed by Mills, came to Cotton Club rehearsals.

segments.chapter: New York, the Lafayette and the Cotton Club
segments.title: Herman Stark and the gangster owners of the Cotton Club
segments.summary: Crawford describes Herman Stark, Owney Madden and Mike Best as the strict owners and says he did not realise they were gangsters.

segments.chapter: New York, the Lafayette and the Cotton Club
segments.title: Joe Jones's outburst at the West End bar
segments.summary: Crawford recalls Joe Jones grabbing his arm when he sat in, and Jones shouting at Matthew Gee for walking in front of him.

segments.chapter: New York, the Lafayette and the Cotton Club
segments.title: Stark's anger at Oxley over the drums
segments.summary: Crawford says Herman Stark once told Oxley to take the band and leave, over the drums Crawford had paid for himself.

segments.chapter: New York, the Lafayette and the Cotton Club
segments.title: The segregated Cotton Club and Bill Robinson's way in
segments.summary: Crawford says the club admitted no Black patrons except Bill Robinson, and entertainers who objected would be fired.

segments.chapter: New York, the Lafayette and the Cotton Club
segments.title: Movie stars, Lena Horne and chorus girls at the Cotton Club
segments.summary: Crawford lists the stars who came in, says musicians could not mingle, and describes chorus girls invited to sit with patrons.

segments.chapter: New York, the Lafayette and the Cotton Club
segments.title: Cotton Club shows versus the Lafayette and Connie's Inn
segments.summary: Crawford insists the Cotton Club's shows were far above the Lafayette's, with the best acts and line.

segments.chapter: New York, the Lafayette and the Cotton Club
segments.title: Waiters' tips, Jack Johnson and Joe Louis at the Cotton Club
segments.summary: Crawford says waiters got the tips, that Jack Johnson first started the club and he later met him, and that Joe Louis got in with Bill Robinson.

segments.chapter: New York, the Lafayette and the Cotton Club
segments.title: Musicians restricted by the club's policy; Cab Calloway
segments.summary: Crawford says only big names like Ellington or Calloway might object to the policy, and says he liked Calloway.

segments.chapter: New York, the Lafayette and the Cotton Club
segments.title: Question about Armstrong and a break in the recording
segments.summary: Crouch asks about Louis Armstrong, then the session pauses to plan the next day.

segments.chapter: Heroes, heard bands and Lunceford's life on the road
segments.title: Louis Armstrong as the idol of trumpeters
segments.summary: Crawford says every trumpeter got something from Armstrong and recalls driving from Memphis to Chicago to hear him.

segments.chapter: Heroes, heard bands and Lunceford's life on the road
segments.title: Buster Bailey, the fastest clarinetist from Memphis
segments.summary: Crawford praises Buster Bailey, who played with W. C. Handy, as the greatest clarinetist, better than Benny Goodman.

segments.chapter: Heroes, heard bands and Lunceford's life on the road
segments.title: John Hammond, Benny Goodman and Basie's swinging band
segments.summary: Crawford says John Hammond's money pushed Goodman and Basie and that Basie had the greatest swinging band.

segments.chapter: Heroes, heard bands and Lunceford's life on the road
segments.title: Basie's relaxed swing versus Crawford's hard digging style
segments.summary: Crawford contrasts his own pushing, digging approach with Basie's smooth natural swing and Jo Jones, and with Chick Webb.

segments.chapter: Heroes, heard bands and Lunceford's life on the road
segments.title: Replacing Walter Conyers in the Army Service Force band
segments.summary: Crawford recalls Walter Conyers, the band's earlier drummer, and the unit led by Clarence Rawls with Joe Turner, Sy Oliver and Bob Carroll.

segments.chapter: Heroes, heard bands and Lunceford's life on the road
segments.title: Lena Horne at the Sands and Sammy Davis's lean days
segments.summary: Crawford tells of the pool being drained after Lena Horne's daughter swam in it and of Sammy Davis eating mustard sandwiches.

segments.chapter: Heroes, heard bands and Lunceford's life on the road
segments.title: What Louis Armstrong was like off the bandstand
segments.summary: Crawford describes Armstrong as jovial and generous, says he rarely played with him, and rejects any Uncle Tom image.

segments.chapter: Heroes, heard bands and Lunceford's life on the road
segments.title: Count Basie and the nickname Steel Chest
segments.summary: Crawford describes Basie mobbed by autograph seekers and calling him Steel Chest.

segments.chapter: Heroes, heard bands and Lunceford's life on the road
segments.title: Growing up with the nickname Jew Baby and neighborhood whippings
segments.summary: Crawford says he was called Jew Baby in Memphis and was beaten by neighbors, then by his grandparents.

segments.chapter: Heroes, heard bands and Lunceford's life on the road
segments.title: Speed Webb's band and McKinney's Cotton Pickers
segments.summary: Crawford praises Speed Webb's swinging band with Roy Eldridge and wonders how McKinney's Cotton Pickers got Don Redman and Cuba Austin.

segments.chapter: Heroes, heard bands and Lunceford's life on the road
segments.title: Big Sid Catlett caught in Boston
segments.summary: Crawford tells of seeing Sid Catlett run naked down Columbus Avenue after being caught in bed with a Jones brother's wife.

segments.chapter: Heroes, heard bands and Lunceford's life on the road
segments.title: Why he admired Sid Catlett's hands, and the match grip
segments.summary: Crawford praises Catlett's natural hands and says modern drummers are noisemakers who hold sticks like clubs; Billy Kyle's drinking comes up.

segments.chapter: Heroes, heard bands and Lunceford's life on the road
segments.title: Records with Goodman and Teddy Wilson, and Quincy Jones's Dinah Washington date
segments.summary: Crawford says he recorded with Benny Goodman and Teddy Wilson, and that Quincy Jones hired him and Milt Hinton for a Dinah Washington album.

segments.chapter: Heroes, heard bands and Lunceford's life on the road
segments.title: Meeting Sid Catlett in the early 1930s and their friendship
segments.summary: Crawford says he met Catlett when he first came to New York and they were jovial friends.

segments.chapter: Heroes, heard bands and Lunceford's life on the road
segments.title: The Lunceford band's baseball team in Central Park
segments.summary: Crawford recalls the band's softball team, Lunceford as pitcher and himself as catcher.

segments.chapter: Heroes, heard bands and Lunceford's life on the road
segments.title: Sy Oliver, Willie Smith and Wilcox on the team and gigs
segments.summary: Crawford says Sy was too delicate for sports, and describes Wilcox's piano playing and the band's gigs.

segments.chapter: Heroes, heard bands and Lunceford's life on the road
segments.title: Why the Lunceford band was so poorly paid
segments.summary: Crawford says the band got at most $65, paid for hotels, uniforms and cleaning, and Sy Oliver got $2 to $4 per arrangement.

segments.chapter: Heroes, heard bands and Lunceford's life on the road
segments.title: Henry Clay, the trumpeter who made him carry his drums home
segments.summary: Crawford recalls the trumpet player Henry Clay, who owned the only car and made him walk a mile home with his drums.

segments.chapter: Heroes, heard bands and Lunceford's life on the road
segments.title: Chick Webb and Buddy Rich
segments.summary: Crawford calls Chick Webb a great boss-drummer whose speed Buddy Rich copied, and says Rich and Sinatra clashed.

segments.chapter: Heroes, heard bands and Lunceford's life on the road
segments.title: Buddy Rich's hands and why Catlett fit any band
segments.summary: Crawford calls Rich the owner of the greatest hands but says Catlett had taste and could fit any band.

segments.chapter: Heroes, heard bands and Lunceford's life on the road
segments.title: How drummers learned their craft
segments.summary: Crawford says drummers either had it or not, and he did not hang out with other drummers.

segments.chapter: Heroes, heard bands and Lunceford's life on the road
segments.title: Sonny Greer in Duke Ellington's band
segments.summary: Crawford says Greer was good only in Ellington's band and describes Freddie Jenkins and other players he noticed.

segments.chapter: Heroes, heard bands and Lunceford's life on the road
segments.title: First hearing Ellington's band in Buffalo
segments.summary: Crawford first heard Ellington's band in Buffalo around 1931-33 and says Lunceford's men went to hear it.

segments.chapter: Heroes, heard bands and Lunceford's life on the road
segments.title: His own long drum solos with stick tricks
segments.summary: Crawford describes drum solos of ten or fifteen minutes with stick twirling that he worked out, though early on he only kept time.

segments.chapter: Heroes, heard bands and Lunceford's life on the road
segments.title: The best drum soloists: Chick Webb, Catlett and Jo Jones
segments.summary: Crawford says Chick Webb outdid them all, including Buddy Rich, and speaks of his fast foot.

segments.chapter: Heroes, rivals and the drummers' craft
segments.title: Recognising drummers by sound and Sonny Greer's flashy style
segments.summary: Crawford says he could identify drummers by sound and that Sonny Greer had a distinctive sound but was suited only to Ellington's band.

segments.chapter: Heroes, rivals and the drummers' craft
segments.title: Sonny Greer's equipment and Gene Krupa's tympani
segments.summary: Crouch and Crawford discuss how Greer's big set-up inspired other drummers to collect equipment.

segments.chapter: Heroes, rivals and the drummers' craft
segments.title: Never studying drums: flash chimes, tympani and Freddy Albright
segments.summary: Crawford says his chimes and tympani were for show, he learned to read through nerve, and he studied late with Freddy Albright.

segments.chapter: The Lunceford years: Europe, rivals and bandsmen
segments.title: Break, and a recap of schooling for drums and football
segments.summary: The recording pauses and Crouch returns to what Crawford said the previous night about school.

segments.chapter: The Lunceford years: Europe, rivals and bandsmen
segments.title: Cap'n Warmack's society band at Willie's Lakeshore Garden
segments.summary: Crawford recalls the Cleveland society band that held the club job during the 1929 strike.

segments.chapter: The Lunceford years: Europe, rivals and bandsmen
segments.title: Highlights of fourteen years: the one-night stands and the Europe trip
segments.summary: Crawford says a job was a job, the band was the biggest one-nighter band, and the European trip was successful.

segments.chapter: The Lunceford years: Europe, rivals and bandsmen
segments.title: Ship's officers befriend Crawford on the way to Europe
segments.summary: Crawford recalls Polish ship officers gathering around him and asking about America.

segments.chapter: The Lunceford years: Europe, rivals and bandsmen
segments.title: Never on dope; drug use among musicians
segments.summary: Crawford says no one in his band used drugs and describes seeing an overdose in the hospital.

segments.chapter: The Lunceford years: Europe, rivals and bandsmen
segments.title: The 1937 Europe tour arranged by Harold Oxley
segments.summary: Crawford says Oxley arranged the 1937 tour and recalls slipping away from Oxley's family for a night out with Al Norris.

segments.chapter: The Lunceford years: Europe, rivals and bandsmen
segments.title: Cities played and no segregation in Europe
segments.summary: Crawford lists Scandinavia and London on the tour and says the band met no segregation and stayed in good white hotels.

segments.chapter: The Lunceford years: Europe, rivals and bandsmen
segments.title: European audiences, dancing and women, and constant touring at home
segments.summary: Audiences in Europe reacted as in America to the band's book, and Crawford says the band toured every whistle stop at home.

segments.chapter: The Lunceford years: Europe, rivals and bandsmen
segments.title: Ballrooms in Bridgeport, Boston and Providence
segments.summary: Crawford says the band played New England ballrooms so often it felt like home and was usually the only band on the stand.

segments.chapter: The Lunceford years: Europe, rivals and bandsmen
segments.title: Tommy Dorsey and circular breathing
segments.summary: Crawford admires Tommy Dorsey's smooth tone and breath control, which Sinatra noticed.

segments.chapter: The Lunceford years: Europe, rivals and bandsmen
segments.title: Benny Goodman's swinging band and quartet
segments.summary: Crawford calls Goodman's band the closest to swing in any white band and lists the quartet.

segments.chapter: The Lunceford years: Europe, rivals and bandsmen
segments.title: Gene Krupa's drumming and showmanship
segments.summary: Crawford loved Krupa as a hard-hitting showman and good friend.

segments.chapter: The Lunceford years: Europe, rivals and bandsmen
segments.title: Alarm-clock pranks on the band bus
segments.summary: Crawford recalls Jack Carruthers and Paul Webster hiding Big Ben alarm clocks in their bags on the bus.

segments.chapter: The Lunceford years: Europe, rivals and bandsmen
segments.title: Willie Smith, the light-skinned society type
segments.summary: Crawford describes Willie Smith's Charleston background and light looks, and begins on Wilcox.

segments.chapter: The Lunceford years: Europe, rivals and bandsmen
segments.title: Second session header for cassettes 3-4, August 1978
segments.summary: Title block for the August 1978 session in Washington.

segments.chapter: The Lunceford years: Europe, rivals and bandsmen
segments.title: Willie Smith passing for white and Lunceford's Fisk education
segments.summary: Crawford says nobody in the band cared that Willie Smith looked white, and he went where the others could not.

segments.chapter: The Lunceford years: Europe, rivals and bandsmen
segments.title: Wilcox the tight-fisted pianist
segments.summary: Crawford describes Wilcox as thrifty, conscientious and devoted to the band, contrasting Freddie Webster.

segments.chapter: The Lunceford years: Europe, rivals and bandsmen
segments.title: Trummy Young practising with a pop bottle
segments.summary: Crawford recalls Trummy Young blowing through a straw in a bottle to learn circular breathing, and says he himself never practised.

segments.chapter: The Lunceford years: Europe, rivals and bandsmen
segments.title: Demanding extra doubles for Broadway shows
segments.summary: Crawford discusses Ernie Royal and Frank West taking Broadway shows and the doubles pay he demanded for percussion.

segments.chapter: The Lunceford years: Europe, rivals and bandsmen
segments.title: Sy Oliver's role in shaping the Lunceford style
segments.summary: Crawford says Sy Oliver contributed more to the Lunceford style than anyone, writing simple arrangements with a beat.

segments.chapter: The Lunceford years: Europe, rivals and bandsmen
segments.title: Underpaid Sy Oliver and the Lunceford-Oxley ownership
segments.summary: Crawford says Sy resented his low pay and that Lunceford turned out to be a hired man whose road manager Dutch Williams handed him money.

segments.chapter: Precision, the union and learning to read
segments.title: Morale, loyalty and hours on the road
segments.summary: Crawford says members gave their hearts to the band and played four to five hours a night.

segments.chapter: Precision, the union and learning to read
segments.title: The band's spontaneous stage show and glee club
segments.summary: Crawford describes trumpets and trombones thrown and caught, saxophones promenading, and the choral arrangements Sy Oliver began.

segments.chapter: Precision, the union and learning to read
segments.title: Why the Lunceford band was so clean and precise
segments.summary: Crawford says the band was the cleanest he heard and credits Lunceford's discipline, Sy Oliver and Willie Smith.

segments.chapter: Precision, the union and learning to read
segments.title: Union 802 required quitting the band; the Army Service Force band
segments.summary: Crawford says 802 would admit them only if they quit the band, then describes two years playing marches at Camp Kilmer.

segments.chapter: Precision, the union and learning to read
segments.title: Italy, Scandinavia and London on the European trip
segments.summary: Crawford says the band toured Scandinavia, went down to Italy and visited London, where he heard imitations of American music.

segments.chapter: Precision, the union and learning to read
segments.title: Hot Lips Page and his wife Elizabeth's cremation
segments.summary: Crawford remembers Page as a warm man who came to talk to him, and relates how Page's former wife was cremated.

segments.chapter: Precision, the union and learning to read
segments.title: Page's advice and the need to read music
segments.summary: Crawford says Page encouraged him to read, and reading was essential for his twenty Broadway musicals.

segments.chapter: Precision, the union and learning to read
segments.title: Reading in the bands and Sy Oliver's drum parts
segments.summary: Crawford explains that Sy relied on his ear and wrote a simple drum part, and that Crawford never tuned his drums.

segments.chapter: Precision, the union and learning to read
segments.title: Symphonic training does not make a swinger
segments.summary: Crawford says symphony-trained players could not swing, and the blues expose anyone who cannot play them.

segments.chapter: Precision, the union and learning to read
segments.title: Teaching himself to read, and the first Broadway musical
segments.summary: Crawford says he taught himself to read drum books and began studying when he started Broadway musicals, around 1949-50 with Alive and Kicking.

segments.chapter: Precision, the union and learning to read
segments.title: Sy Oliver wrote out drum parts as a guide
segments.summary: Crawford says Sy Oliver wrote a drum part for everyone with accents marked, which taught him he had to read.

segments.chapter: Precision, the union and learning to read
segments.title: The blues as the test of a drummer's education
segments.summary: Crawford says anyone who cannot play the blues, with brushes or sticks, will not fit, and longhair-trained players fail at it.

segments.chapter: Blues, riverboats and drumming craft
segments.title: Favorite blues singers: Bessie Smith, Ma Rainey, Billie Holiday
segments.summary: Crawford names the blues singers he heard at the Palace Theatre and later ones such as Dinah Washington and Billie Holiday, and the rise of Sinatra.

segments.chapter: Blues, riverboats and drumming craft
segments.title: Bing Crosby's influence on singers of the 1930s
segments.summary: Crouch asks about Crosby's influence on singers like Sy Oliver, and Crawford says Crosby influenced Sinatra and others.

segments.chapter: Blues, riverboats and drumming craft
segments.title: The blues drum beat and Mississippi riverboat bands at Memphis
segments.summary: Crawford recalls hearing riverboat bands with blues trumpets and trombones from the Memphis levee.

segments.chapter: Blues, riverboats and drumming craft
segments.title: African drummers and the independence of limbs
segments.summary: Crawford says African drummers have great independence, which he had to study hard to match.

segments.chapter: Blues, riverboats and drumming craft
segments.title: Riverboat drummers' press rolls and Bubber Miley's plunger
segments.summary: Crawford says the riverboat drummers played press rolls and four on the bass drum, and credits Bubber Miley with the plunger sound.

segments.chapter: Blues, riverboats and drumming craft
segments.title: Why drummers dropped traps; Sonny Greer and Buddy Rich
segments.summary: Crawford says Sonny Greer upset the old effects set-up and calls Buddy Rich the greatest snare drummer ever.

segments.chapter: Blues, riverboats and drumming craft
segments.title: Favorite bass players: Milt Hinton, Pettiford and Jimmy Blanton
segments.summary: Crawford names Milt Hinton first, praises Oscar Pettiford and Jimmy Blanton, and marvels at Ellington's men.

segments.chapter: Blues, riverboats and drumming craft
segments.title: John Kirby's group and McKinney's Cotton Pickers
segments.summary: Crawford discusses John Kirby's small band showing Lunceford's influence and wonders how McKinney's Cotton Pickers gathered such musicians.

segments.chapter: Blues, riverboats and drumming craft
segments.title: Brush playing and Sid Catlett's brush solos
segments.summary: Crawford says he played waltzes with brushes and names Sid Catlett as the best brush man.

segments.chapter: Blues, riverboats and drumming craft
segments.title: Fast tempos were hardest, and learning to cheat on cymbals
segments.summary: Crawford says fast tempos with the bass drum scared him, recalls a moment at the Apollo, and describes cheating with the cymbals.

segments.chapter: Blues, riverboats and drumming craft
segments.title: The best tempo keepers
segments.summary: Crawford names Cupie Austin, Sid Catlett, Jo Jones and Kaiser Marshall as the best tempo men.

segments.chapter: Blues, riverboats and drumming craft
segments.title: Fletcher Henderson's many keys again
segments.summary: Crawford repeats that Henderson wrote in all keys and it took Roy Eldridge a long time to adjust.

segments.chapter: Blues, riverboats and drumming craft
segments.title: Jelly Roll Morton, riverboat bands and Alphonso Trent's sidemen
segments.summary: Crawford never met Jelly Roll Morton, recalls the levee bands, and describes Alphonso Trent's sidemen such as banjoist Crooke.

segments.chapter: Road life, segregation and band pranks
segments.title: Musicians' hangouts: the Rhythm Club and neighboring bars
segments.summary: Crawford lists the Rhythm Club and nearby bars where musicians met to talk.

segments.chapter: Road life, segregation and band pranks
segments.title: One-nighters and segregation: hotels, cleaners and the Cotton Club
segments.summary: Crawford says the band travelled nightly, hated segregation and could stay only in cheap colored hotels.

segments.chapter: Road life, segregation and band pranks
segments.title: Colored restaurants and the danger of interracial romance
segments.summary: Crawford says bands always knew the colored restaurants and avoided white women because of lynching, and mentions his long marriage.

segments.chapter: Road life, segregation and band pranks
segments.title: Musicians sharing tips on where to eat, sleep and clean clothes
segments.summary: Crawford says bands exchanged information on places to stay and eat, and repeats the 1929 Lakeside and Cleveland strike story.

segments.chapter: Road life, segregation and band pranks
segments.title: How people viewed musicians and the Lunceford band's reputation
segments.summary: Crawford says musicians were seen as an ordinary profession, but the Lunceford band, Ellington and Calloway were looked up to.

segments.chapter: Road life, segregation and band pranks
segments.title: Junior Raglin, Barney Bigard and the bottle prank
segments.summary: Crawford tells how Bigard tricked the kleptomaniac bassist Junior Raglin into drinking from a bottle of urine.

segments.chapter: Road life, segregation and band pranks
segments.title: More on the alarm-clock jokers Carruthers and Webster
segments.summary: Crawford repeats the alarm clock prank by Jack Carruthers and Paul Webster on the bus.

segments.chapter: Road life, segregation and band pranks
segments.title: Willie Smith's constant reading and his cigarette ritual
segments.summary: Crawford describes Willie Smith always reading and saying a prayer before handing over a cigarette.

segments.chapter: Politics, bebop and the small-band years
segments.title: Musicians' politics, voting and the presidents
segments.summary: Crawford says the musicians took little interest in politics or voting until Roosevelt, and he praises Truman and Carter.

segments.chapter: Politics, bebop and the small-band years
segments.title: African-themed tunes and tom-tom ballads of the late 1930s
segments.summary: Crouch asks about pieces with African titles and mallets on tom-toms, and Crawford vaguely recalls playing such rhythms.

segments.chapter: Politics, bebop and the small-band years
segments.title: Latin rhythms, Machito and Mario Bauza
segments.summary: Crawford says Lunceford played little Latin music, and recalls Machito and trumpeter Mario Bauza.

segments.chapter: Politics, bebop and the small-band years
segments.title: Studying on the practice pad in the Army and marches turning to swing
segments.summary: Crawford says he practised marches on the practice pad he took into the Army in 1942 and recalls his fellow drummer Buster.

segments.chapter: Politics, bebop and the small-band years
segments.title: Peeking through the crack at Cafe Society's drummer
segments.summary: After the Army, Crawford was sent to Ed Hall at Cafe Society and watched drummer Trap Hull play the show from outside.

segments.chapter: Politics, bebop and the small-band years
segments.title: Playing in a small band versus a big band, with Ed Hall for five years
segments.summary: Crawford says a small-band drummer is exposed and must fit in with taste and touch, and he took only breaks in Ed Hall's band for about five years.

segments.chapter: Politics, bebop and the small-band years
segments.title: Disliking bebop; Art Blakey, Max Roach and Kenny Clarke
segments.summary: Crawford says he preferred swinging and did not care for bebop but admired Blakey, Roach and his friend Kenny Clarke.

segments.chapter: Politics, bebop and the small-band years
segments.title: Meeting Dizzy Gillespie in Philadelphia
segments.summary: Crawford says he met Dizzy in Philadelphia, credits him with bringing in bebop, and calls him a great all-around trumpeter who could swing.

segments.chapter: Politics, bebop and the small-band years
segments.title: What bothered him about bebop drummers
segments.summary: Crawford says bebop drummers got out of hand and called it noise, naming Clarke and Roach as all-around drummers and Roy Haynes a combo drummer.

segments.chapter: Politics, bebop and the small-band years
segments.title: Working with Ben Webster and his dislike of Billy Taylor
segments.summary: Crawford says Ben Webster wanted a swinging piano and could not stand Billy Taylor's style, but they otherwise got along.

segments.chapter: Politics, bebop and the small-band years
segments.title: Working with Sidney Bechet
segments.summary: Crawford names Benny Goodman and Sidney Bechet among his small-group jobs and says Bechet was tough to work for.

segments.chapter: Politics, bebop and the small-band years
segments.title: How the New York scene changed after the war
segments.summary: Crawford says guys stopped swinging and he had to relearn his approach to music.

segments.chapter: Politics, bebop and the small-band years
segments.title: Jim Chapin's drum book and independence in bebop
segments.summary: Crawford says exercises from Chapin's book helped his technique and independence, which bebop introduced to drumming.

segments.chapter: Broadway, studio work and close
segments.title: Billy Kyle gets him into Broadway musicals
segments.summary: Billy Kyle, a rehearsal pianist, recommended Crawford as a swinging drummer who could read, which led to over twenty musicals.

segments.chapter: Broadway, studio work and close
segments.title: Studying rudiments and xylophone after starting the shows
segments.summary: Crawford began weekly lessons on rudiments on the practice pad and studied xylophone to become a percussionist.

segments.chapter: Broadway, studio work and close
segments.title: The pit orchestra: reading, being the only Black player and swinging the longhairs
segments.summary: Crawford says the shows were a challenge, he was usually the only Black musician, and directors wanted him to make classical players swing.

segments.chapter: Broadway, studio work and close
segments.title: Studio and television work, and only two Black drummers on Broadway
segments.summary: Crawford recorded for many stars and television shows and says only he and Specs Powell were Black drummers doing that work.

segments.chapter: Broadway, studio work and close
segments.title: Recording with Perry Como, Mitch Miller and Jackie Gleason
segments.summary: Crawford recalls Perry Como's Kokomo, work for Mitch Miller and Jackie Gleason, and supporting the longhairs with Bobby Hackett.

segments.chapter: Broadway, studio work and close
segments.title: Quincy Jones's Dinah Washington date
segments.summary: Crawford repeats that Quincy Jones hired him and Milt Hinton for a Dinah Washington date because he wanted drummers who just play.

segments.chapter: Broadway, studio work and close
segments.title: Crawford tires and asks that gaps be bracketed
segments.summary: Crawford says he is tired, will eat and nap, and asks Crouch to bracket any shortcomings in the tapes.

segments.chapter: Broadway, studio work and close
segments.title: Retirement, and musicians who scorned Broadway shows
segments.summary: Crouch asks about his retirement, and Crawford says musicians who looked down on Broadway shows later sought them.

segments.chapter: Broadway, studio work and close
segments.title: His book 'I Did the Very Best I Could' and Stanley Dance
segments.summary: Crawford says he has nearly finished a memoir, with several publishers interested, and praises Stanley Dance.

segments.chapter: Broadway, studio work and close
segments.title: Yacht caps and summers in Atlantic City
segments.summary: Crawford explains why he wore captain's caps at Atlantic City, where Basie and Lennie Hayton did too.

segments.chapter: Broadway, studio work and close
segments.title: Closing thanks to the Smithsonian
segments.summary: Crouch thanks Crawford, estimates five hours of material, and Crawford thanks the Smithsonian.
